source.title: How to Create an Emergency Water Supply
source.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (National Center for Environmental Health)
source.supports: 1 gallon per person per day for 3 days; try for 2 weeks; more for pregnancy, illness, pets, heat; container cleaning (1 tsp unscented bleach per quart, 30 seconds); replace stored water every 6 months; unscented bleach 5-9% sodium hypochlorite.
source.notes: Page metadata also shows a 2026-04-24 republish; the visible 'Updated/Reviewed' date is 2025-06-27.

source.title: How to Make Water Safe in an Emergency
source.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (National Center for Environmental Health)
source.supports: Boil 1 minute (3 above 6,500 ft); clear cloudy water first; bleach tables (5-9% and 1%); wait 30 minutes; chemical disinfectants weaker against Cryptosporidium and Giardia; chlorine dioxide tablets vs Cryptosporidium; iodine cautions; filter pore sizes 0.3 and 1 micron, viruses not removed; UV and solar disinfection limits; cannot make water containing fuel, toxic chemicals or radioactive materials safe by boiling or disinfecting; never drink radiator or boiler water.
source.notes: Page metadata shows a 2025-12-18 republish; visible 'Updated/Reviewed' date is 2024-09-19.

source.title: Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water
source.publisher: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (Office of Water)
source.supports: Independent cross-check of CDC: boil at least 1 minute, 3 minutes above 5,000 ft; 8 drops of 6% bleach per gallon, double if cloudy/colored/cold, stand 30 minutes; do not use scented, color-safe or added-cleaner bleach; bleach stored at room temperature under 1 year; boiling/disinfection do not destroy heavy metals, salts and most chemicals; Safe Drinking Water Hotline 1-800-426-4791.
source.notes: DISCREPANCY with CDC: EPA's high-altitude boiling threshold is 5,000 ft; CDC's is 6,500 ft. Page metadata lists a future review date (2027-02-24), which is a schedule, not a past review.

source.title: Botulism Prevention
source.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (NCEZID)
source.supports: Common botulism sources are improperly canned, preserved or fermented homemade foods; toxin cannot be seen, smelled or tasted; pressure canning is the only recommended method for low-acid foods; 'If in doubt, throw it out'.

source.title: Clostridium botulinum & Botulism
source.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
source.supports: Botulism has been linked to traditionally prepared salted or fermented fish; nitrites in cured meat inhibit C. botulinum spore growth; USDA authorized nitrite in meat and poultry beginning 1925; early-1970s nitrosamine concern; spores survive boiling, pressure needed for low-acid foods; symptoms and urgency.

source.title: How do I safely cure meats at home to avoid botulism?
source.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service (Ask USDA)
source.supports: Many botulism cases followed home-canned, preserved, curing, smoking or fermented foods contaminated with toxin. Short article; it points to the NCHFP for method detail and gives no home curing formula.

source.title: Curing & Smoking
source.publisher: National Center for Home Food Preservation (University of Georgia, USDA-supported)
source.supports: Describes curing as using salt (and sometimes sugar) to draw moisture from meat and discourage harmful microorganisms, and as a matter of balancing time, temperature and ingredients.
source.notes: This is a topic index page with a short description, not a tested procedure. No curing formulas are taken from it.

source.title: Food and Drink in the U.S. Navy, 1794 to 1820
source.supports: 1813 provisions load-out and weekly ration table; 1812 Binney contract specification for beef and pork; steeping of salt meat; bread/biscuit contract and dimensions; 'hardtack' as a 1840s term; pests; water rules (1802 regulations); Porter on water casks. Cites primary records (NARA contracts, ship journals, Naval Regulations 1802) in footnotes.
source.notes: Secondary study built on primary records. Its footnotes are the route to the primary documents; those have not yet been pulled individually.

source.title: Life at sea in the age of sail
source.supports: Main rations were salt beef or pork, cheese, fish, ale and ship's biscuit; food quality worsened with poor storage, ventilation and vermin; scurvy caused by lack of vitamin C.
source.notes: Short overview with no quantities or dates for the ration.

source.title: Ship's Biscuit (AAB0766)
source.publisher: Royal Museums Greenwich, National Maritime Museum
source.supports: A ship's biscuit made to an 1846 recipe, marked with a broad arrow and the letter C; wheat; measurements 15 x 135 mm; not on display.
source.notes: Image rights are held by RMG (licensing offered). No RMG image is used in this archive.

source.title: Life Aboard (On the Water: Fishing for a Living)
source.publisher: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
source.supports: Gloucester schooner Ocean King, 1879 Grand Banks voyage, cook George W. Scott's journal list of provisions for a four-month voyage, including 210 hogsheads of salt for salting cod, 5 barrels beef, 1 barrel pork, 1 barrel hams.

source.title: A treatise of the scurvy, in three parts (James Lind, 1753)
source.publisher: Smithsonian Libraries and Archives (digitized, no known copyright)
source.supports: Digitized primary source: first published 1753; full text and PDF available through the Internet Archive item. Library catalogue note says more sailors were dying from scurvy than from combat when it appeared.
source.notes: The drafting agent read the catalogue record, not the 456-page text. Page-level claims from the Treatise are NOT made in articles.

source.title: James Lind and scurvy: 1747 to 1795
source.publisher: The James Lind Library (Ulrich Troehler, 2003; republished J R Soc Med 2005;98:519-522)
source.supports: Lind's 1747 comparison aboard HMS Salisbury (80 of 350 sailors struck by scurvy in a ten-week cruise; 12 patients, six treatments); Sick and Hurt Board rejected a fruit-juice proposal the year after the Treatise; 'rob' made by heating destroyed much ascorbic acid; 1795 Admiralty sanction of lemon juice; a lag the author counts as 42 years.

source.title: Drinking Water Advisories: An Overview
source.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (National Center for Environmental Health)
source.supports: Three advisory types (boil water, do not drink, do not use) and what each asks of a household; do not use fridge water or ice dispensers during any advisory; boil tap water even if filtered; infant feeding, handwashing, bathing, brushing teeth, dishes (150 F dishwasher; 1 tsp unscented bleach per gallon soak), laundry, cleaning, pets, gardens; boiling does not fix chemicals or toxins; do-not-use advisories are rare.
source.notes: The page's visible 'Updated' date (Feb 21, 2024) precedes its 'Published' date (Sep 16, 2024); both recorded as shown. Page metadata shows a 2025-06-25 republish.

source.title: How to Find Clean Water in an Emergency
source.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (National Center for Environmental Health)
source.supports: Other water inside the home (tap water heater tank, melted ice cubes, clear untreated toilet tank water, liquid from canned fruit and vegetables, pool/spa water for hygiene only); outdoor sources (rainwater, streams, ponds, springs) must be treated; contaminated-by-fuel-or-chemicals water cannot be made safe; may need to shut the main water valve.

source.title: About Water Treatment Options When Hiking, Camping, or Traveling
source.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (NCEZID)
source.supports: Clear water can be unsafe; boiling best; filter then disinfect next best; absolute pore sizes (1 micron parasites; 0.3 micron bacteria and parasites; viruses not removed) or NSF 53/58 cyst certification; reverse osmosis removes parasites, bacteria, viruses and salt; chlorine dioxide vs parasites; UV needs clear water; iodine cautions.

source.title: Two Ways to Purify Water
source.supports: Never drink untreated natural water even if clear; filtration by itself does not purify water and must be followed by boiling or disinfection; filters are screens that cannot remove viruses; filter cloudy water even if you will boil it; filter care per manufacturer; pool-cleaning tablets must not be used; consult a physician about iodine; boiling 1 min (3 min above 6,500 ft) works even on cloudy water; UV is for small quantities of clear water.

source.title: Water
source.supports: At least one gallon per person per day for drinking and sanitation; normal active person needs about three quarters of a gallon of fluid; more for children, nursing mothers, sick people, medical emergencies, warm climates (need can double); never ration drinking water unless ordered; avoid carbonated and caffeinated substitutes; bottled water in sealed original containers, cool and dark; replace non-commercial stored water every six months; settle or strain before treating; boiling; bleach 5.25-6% only (1/8 tsp per gallon); distillation removes microbes, heavy metals, salts and most chemicals.
source.notes: DISCREPANCIES with CDC: Ready.gov limits bleach to 5.25-6.0% and says iodine and camping-store treatments 'are not recommended'; CDC accepts 5-9% bleach plus iodine and chlorine dioxide products. Page is older (updated 2021).

source.title: Prepare Your Pets for Disasters
source.supports: Pets belong in the household plan; two pet kits (shelter and evacuation); store a water bowl and several days' supply of water for pets; no per-pet water quantity is given.
source.notes: No numerical pet water allowance in this source. Do not invent one.

source.title: How do you keep food safe during a power failure?
source.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service (Ask USDA)
source.supports: A refrigerator keeps food cold for about 4 hours if unopened; a full stand-alone freezer holds temperature about 48 hours (24 if half full) with the door closed; a refrigerator's freezer compartment may not hold as long; group freezer packages together.
source.notes: Short Q&A that points to the longer FSIS emergencies page. Upgraded from the register placeholder.

source.title: What foods should I keep in my house for emergencies?
source.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service (Ask USDA)
source.supports: Keep nonperishable food and a 3-day supply of commercially bottled water per person (minimum 3 gallons); example foods; choose small cans so there are no leftovers needing refrigeration; include infant formula, pet food and special-diet foods; have a manual can opener; periodically use and refresh the supply.
source.notes: Upgraded from the register placeholder. The first fetch returned only the page title; a second fetch with a render wait returned the full text.

source.title: National Center for Home Food Preservation
source.supports: Describes itself as the source of current research-based recommendations for most methods of home food preservation, established with USDA funding to address food-safety concerns; sections on canning, pickling, fermenting, freezing, drying, curing and smoking, and storing.
source.notes: Home page only. Used as the hub link. Upgraded from the register placeholder.

source.title: Jerky
source.publisher: NCHFP, University of Georgia (extracted from So Easy to Preserve, 6th ed.)
source.supports: Jerky safety procedure: raw poultry generally not recommended; freeze pork and wild game 6 inches or thinner at 0 F or below for at least 30 days against trichinella; handling rules; wild-game cautions; reaching 160 F internally by heating in marinade before drying or in an oven after drying, without case hardening; slices no thicker than 1/4 inch; dry in a dehydrator or oven preheated to 140 F until a test piece cracks but does not break; ground-meat jerky is harder; home-dried jerky keeps 2 weeks at room temperature in a sealed container, longer refrigerated or frozen.
source.notes: Page text credits "So Easy to Preserve", 6th ed. 2014 (Bulletin 989, UGA Cooperative Extension). No page-level date is shown. Upgraded from the register placeholder.

source.title: Meat, Ground or Chopped (pressure canning)
source.publisher: NCHFP, University of Georgia (adapted from the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning)
source.supports: A tested pressure-canning process for ground or chopped meat: it must be read with Using Pressure Canners; process time varies by jar size, and canner pressure varies by dial-gauge versus weighted-gauge canner and by elevation band (separate tables). The tables are NOT reproduced in the article.
source.notes: Page text says it was adapted from the Complete Guide to Home Canning, Agriculture Information Bulletin No. 539, USDA, revised 2015. Upgraded from the register placeholder.

source.title: Keep Your Food Safe During Emergencies: Power Outages, Floods & Fires
source.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
source.supports: Power-outage planning (appliance thermometers: refrigerator 40 F or below, freezer 0 F or below; group and fill the freezer; cooler and gel packs); refrigerator safe up to 4 hours; full freezer about 48 hours (24 half full); 50 lb dry ice holds an 18 cu ft freezer 2 days; do not put perishable food in snow; never taste food to judge safety; lists of foods to discard after more than 4 hours without power and foods that are safe; frozen-food rules; flood and fire guidance; USDA Meat and Poultry Hotline 1-888-674-6854.
source.notes: Visible 'Last Updated' is Aug 07, 2013; it is the older, longer FSIS page and the shorter Ask USDA articles point to it. Its bleach sanitizing amounts (1 tablespoon per gallon) differ from CDC's and Ready.gov's.

source.title: Keep Food Safe After a Disaster or Emergency
source.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (NCEZID)
source.supports: Appliance thermometers (refrigerator 40 F or below, freezer 0 F or below); doors closed; food safe up to 4 hours in a refrigerator, 48 hours in a full freezer, 24 hours in a half-full freezer; move perishables to a cooler with a cold source at 4 hours; throw out perishables after 4 hours without power or a cold source; never taste food to judge safety; refreeze or cook thawed food that still has ice crystals or is 40 F or below; flood-food and canned-food steps including its own bleach solution amounts.
source.notes: Its bleach sanitizing amounts (1 cup per 5 gallons) differ from FSIS and FDA (1 tablespoon per gallon) and Ready.gov (1 part bleach to 10 parts water). Not reproduced in the articles.

source.title: Food Safety During Power Outage (charts)
source.publisher: FoodSafety.gov (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services)
source.supports: Refrigerator keeps food safe up to 4 hours; item-by-item keep-or-discard chart for refrigerated food exposed to 40 F or above for more than 2 hours; item-by-item refreeze-or-discard chart for frozen food (ice crystals versus above 40 F for more than 2 hours); full freezer 48 hours, half full 24; never taste food to judge safety.
source.notes: Visible 'Date Last Reviewed' is August 8, 2024; page metadata shows a 2024-08-15 modification. The chart's 2-hour column and the 4-hour refrigerator rule are two different clocks that readers often merge.

source.title: Food and Water Safety During Power Outages and Floods
source.supports: Prepare: appliance thermometers, freeze water containers (melting ice can also supply drinking water), freeze items, group freezer food, coolers, ice, dry or block ice; during: refrigerator about 4 hours, full freezer about 48 hours, 50 lb dry ice holds an 18 cu ft freezer two days; cook meat, poultry, fish, eggs to a safe minimum internal temperature; discard perishables held at room temperature 2 hours or more (1 hour above 90 F); after: refrigerated perishables above 40 F for 4 hours or more should be discarded, and perishables at 45 F or below measured with a food thermometer should be safe but cooked and eaten promptly; foodborne-illness symptoms and timing (20 minutes to 6 weeks); flood food and water steps.
source.notes: Page metadata shows a 2024-03-05 modification and a 2025-02-25 publication, which look inconsistent; both recorded as shown. The 45 F allowance appears here but not in the FSIS, CDC or Ready.gov pages we read. Its bleach amounts are 1 tablespoon per gallon of 5.25% bleach for utensils and counters but 1 cup in 5 gallons for cans; FSIS uses 1 tablespoon per gallon for cans and CDC 1 cup in 5 gallons throughout.

source.title: Food
source.supports: Store at least a several-day supply of non-perishable food; choose foods your family will eat; special dietary needs; example items including a manual can opener; do not eat from swollen, dented or corroded cans; throw away food at room temperature two hours or more; refrigerator about four hours unopened; discard perishables above 40 F for two hours or more; dry ice 25 lb for a 10 cu ft freezer three to four days, gloves, no direct contact with food; heating canned food and a bleach-to-water disinfecting ratio.
source.notes: Its dry-ice figure (25 lb, 10 cu ft, three to four days) and its 'two hours or more above 40 F' rule differ in framing from FSIS and FDA. Its can-disinfecting ratio (1 part bleach to 10 parts water) differs from FSIS, FDA and CDC. Newer FEMA material (fact sheet V-1008, December 2023) states the discard rule as 'exposed to temperatures 40 degrees Fahrenheit or higher for more than 4 hours', not two hours; see food-fema-outage-sheet.

source.title: Shelf-Stable Food Safety
source.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
source.supports: What shelf stable means; canned-food shelf-life limits (rust, dents, heat above 100 F; below 85 F best; check the pantry every few weeks and use older cans); discard heavily rusted, deeply dented, swollen, spurting cans; accidentally frozen cans; botulism in canned goods, spores, symptoms in 12 to 48 hours; precautions for home-canned foods (boil low-acid and tomato foods 10 minutes, plus 1 minute per 1,000 ft, not a guarantee); dating is not required and is about quality; can codes are not use-by dates; drying and jerky temperature; home-dried jerky shelf life 1 to 2 months; storage chart.
source.notes: INTERNAL CONFLICT: its storage chart says home-canned foods keep 12 months and to boil 10 minutes (high-acid) or 20 minutes (low-acid) before using, while its own text says boil low-acid and tomato foods 10 minutes plus 1 minute per 1,000 ft and that properly home-canned fruits never needed the boil. CDC's page agrees with the text, not the chart. Read in full (main content) 2026-10-29.

source.title: Food Product Dating
source.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
source.supports: Product dating is not required by federal law except for infant formula; dates indicate quality, not safety; meaning of Best if Used By, Sell-By, Use-By, Freeze-By; foods without spoilage signs are wholesome past the date if handled properly; infant formula Use-By is regulated and formula should not be used after it; can codes are not Best-if-Used-By dates; high-acid canned foods keep best quality 12 to 18 months, low-acid 2 to 5 years; donation after the date; USDA Meat and Poultry Hotline hours.
source.notes: A can's 'closed' code and an 'open' calendar date are different things on the same can.

source.title: FoodKeeper App
source.publisher: FoodSafety.gov (HHS); developed by USDA FSIS with Cornell University and the Food Marketing Institute
source.supports: The FoodKeeper is a searchable storage-guidance tool, also available as a mobile app, developed by USDA FSIS with Cornell University and the Food Marketing Institute, covering categories including shelf-stable foods.
source.notes: READ SCOPE: landing text and category list only, not individual entries. No storage durations are taken from it.

source.title: Room Temperature Storage
source.supports: Pantry tips (keep storage dry, off the ground, apart from cleaning supplies, cover opened food against pests, do not use swollen cans, rotate first in first out); meaning of package dates including pack dates and expiration dates; points to the USDA FoodKeeper.
source.notes: No page date shown.

source.title: Storing Canned Goods
source.supports: Commercially canned food is superior to home canned for food storage; label purchase month and year; store cool, dark, dry, off the floor, away from furnaces, pipes and attics; do not let cans or jars freeze; first in first out; discard dented, bulging, rusty or leaky cans; shelf-life general rules; it suggests tasting a sample of older canned food that looks and smells normal.
source.notes: CONFLICT: its suggestion to taste a sample and its boiling advice for older canned food (heat low-acid food to 165 F or boil 5 to 10 minutes) differ from CDC and FSIS ('never taste', boil 10 minutes plus 1 minute per 1,000 ft). No page date shown; references run to 2006.

source.title: Survival Basics: Food - How to Stock Up and Prepare for Natural Disasters (EM 9331)
source.supports: Eat refrigerated food first, then frozen, then pantry; store food your family will eat so you can cycle through it; add a little each shop and use sales; inspect stored food for pests every six months with a calendar alert; storage locations and small-home tips; two-week and four-week targets are Oregon planning figures; after the refrigerator passes 40 F most refrigerated foods keep no longer than two more hours; home-canning cautions including that vacuum-sealing low-acid foods stored at room temperature can create an environment for botulism toxin; do not can water, butter, dairy, grains, leftovers, cakes, quick breads or cured meats.
source.notes: Written for the Cascadia earthquake scenario; the 2-week and 4-week supply targets are Oregon-specific. The 'updated' date is page metadata. It says eggs can be kept at room temperature up to six days unless washed or cooked, which most store eggs have been; we do not repeat it.

source.title: Jerky and Food Safety
source.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
source.supports: Pathogenic bacteria are likely to survive dry heat and the 130 to 140 F of a food dehydrator; Salmonella and E. coli O157:H7 illnesses from homemade jerky; USDA Hotline recommendation to heat meat to 160 F and poultry to 165 F before dehydrating, then dry at a constant 130 to 140 F; why the order matters (evaporation keeps the meat cool, bacteria become more heat resistant); sun drying not recommended; summary of a 2004 Journal of Food Protection study (marination alone did not reduce the pathogen; E. coli survived up to 10 hours at up to 145 F in lab-inoculated venison) and a 1998 study on ground beef jerky with and without a nitrite curing mix; wild-game contamination; storage times (commercial 12 months, home-dried 1 to 2 months).
source.notes: Studies are reported as FSIS summarizes them; we did not read the journal articles. Currency check 2026-10-30 in a browser: the page still shows 'Last Updated: Nov 03, 2016' and the same 160 F / 165 F, 130 to 140 F and 1 to 2 months figures as the newer Ask USDA article (Feb 2025). Kansas State MF3173 cites an FSIS 'Jerky and Food Safety' fact sheet dated September 22, 2023 at a /meat/jerky path; we could not retrieve that version (automated fetch refused), so we cannot say whether it differs.

source.title: How can I make meat or poultry jerky at home?
source.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service (Ask USDA)
source.supports: Current USDA Hotline recommendation: heat meat to 160 F and poultry to 165 F before dehydrating (steam or roast, checked with a food thermometer); dehydrator with an adjustable temperature dial that holds 130 to 140 F throughout drying; dry until a test piece cracks but does not break; 10 to 24 hours when not heated in marinade; seven handling steps.
source.notes: Newer than the longer FSIS fact sheet (2016 date) and consistent with it.

source.title: Dehydrating Meat Safely at Home (MF3173)
source.publisher: Kansas State University Research and Extension
source.supports: USDA recommendation to heat meat to 160 F and poultry to 165 F; a dehydrator may not reach those temperatures; keep dehydrator at 130 to 140 F and do not raise it to rush drying because higher heat causes case hardening; the two NCHFP heating methods; ground-meat jerky needs 160 F, heat 10 minutes in an oven after dehydrating; raw poultry not recommended for jerky for texture and flavor; homemade jerky best used within 1 to 2 months, refrigerate or freeze for longer.
source.notes: Revised March 2026 per the publication. Cites the NCHFP, FSIS and NDSU pages. Its 1-to-2-month storage figure agrees with FSIS and disagrees with NCHFP's 2 weeks.

source.title: Using Pressure Canners
source.supports: Dial versus weighted gauges; UL-approved canners only; a canner should hold at least 4 quart jars to be a pressure canner for USDA processes; serious errors from not adjusting for elevation, air trapped in the canner (vent 10 minutes before pressurizing) and an inaccurate dial gauge (check yearly; replace if off by more than 2 pounds at 5, 10 or 15 pounds); step-by-step operation; if pressure drops, restart the full timing; do not force-cool; jars sit 12 to 24 hours; burner cautions.
source.notes: This page says the canner pressurizes 'during the next 3 to 10 minutes'; the NCHFP 'How to Use Boiling Water and Pressure Canners' page says 3 to 5. Minor, but recorded.

source.title: Ensuring Safe Canned Foods
source.publisher: NCHFP, University of Georgia (adapted from the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning, rev. 2015)
source.supports: Botulism growth conditions (moist low-acid food, 40 to 120 F, under 2 percent oxygen, toxin in 3 to 4 days); spores harmless on fresh food because they need an airless environment; low-acid foods have pH above 4.6 and include red meats, seafood, poultry, milk and all fresh vegetables except most tomatoes; low-acid foods must be sterilized at 240 to 250 F in pressure canners at 10 to 15 PSIG; the time range for low-acid food in a boiling-water canner is 7 to 11 hours; use the recommended research-based times; altitude of 1,000 ft or more needs adjusted processes; store below 95 F (50 to 70 F for quality).
source.notes: Washing fresh food reduces microorganisms only slightly; peeling and blanching help; method and tested times are the vital controls.

source.title: How to Use Boiling Water and Pressure Canners
source.publisher: NCHFP, University of Georgia (adapted from the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning)
source.supports: Low-acid foods must be processed in a pressure canner to be free of botulism risks; pressure does not destroy microorganisms, temperature held long enough does; at sea level 10.5 lb gauge pressure gives 240 F; elevation and trapped air are the two serious errors; venting; weighted-gauge limits above 1,000 ft; dial gauges checked each year, counties' Cooperative Extension offices may test them; pressure saucepans with smaller capacity are not recommended; the 10-step pressure-canner routine.
source.notes: Page text says it was adapted from the Complete Guide, 'revised 2009'. It says the canner pressurizes in 3 to 5 minutes; the NCHFP 'Using Pressure Canners' page says 3 to 10.

source.title: Canning in Electric Multi-Cookers (Newsflash)
source.supports: NCHFP does not support the use of USDA canning processes in electric multi-cooker appliances, even those with canning or steam-canning buttons, and gives four reasons: no thermal-process work with jars inside them, temperature (not pressure) is what matters, temperature must stay at minimum through the process, and USDA low-acid processes count heat from coming up to pressure and from natural cooling.
source.notes: Dated February 1, 2019. Excludes the Ball electric boiling-water-style canner for acid foods.

source.title: Dry Canning Raw Vegetables is an Unsafe Practice
source.supports: Pressure canning raw vegetables in jars with no added liquid is potentially very hazardous; the covering liquid is required for heat penetration; bacteria die more slowly in dry heat; butter or ghee are no substitute; botulism toxin may be present with no visible or odor change; research-based processes must be used as written, including altitude adjustments.
source.notes: A blog post, not a regulation, but from the NCHFP and referring to the USDA hotline calls it was prompted by.

source.title: Equipment and Methods Not Recommended (Canning)
source.publisher: NCHFP, University of Georgia (from the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning)
source.supports: Open-kettle canning and processing filled jars in conventional ovens, microwave ovens and dishwashers are not recommended; canning powders are useless as preservatives; pressure above 15 PSI not recommended for new equipment; 'dry canning' of vegetables without covering liquid and 'dry canning' of dry foods by heating jars in an oven are not recommended; steam canners are described as not currently recommended, with a pointer to newer atmospheric steam-canner guidance.
source.notes: STALE-TEXT NOTE: this page still says steam canners are not currently recommended, while a September 2026 NCHFP newsflash calls atmospheric steam canning safe for high-acid foods when tested recipes and steps are followed. Neither concerns low-acid foods.

source.title: Atmospheric Steam Canning Statement (Newsflash)
source.supports: NCHFP considers atmospheric steam canning a safe method for high-acid foods (fruits, jams, pickles, tomatoes) when tested recipes and guidelines are followed; it says nothing that extends this to low-acid foods.
source.notes: Dated 'September 2026' on the page. The URL slug contains a typo ('tatement') and is reproduced as is.

source.title: Home-Canned Foods (Botulism Prevention)
source.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (NCEZID)
source.supports: Follow the USDA Complete Guide; do not use other recipes even from a trusted friend or relative; low-acid foods (pH above 4.6) are the most common source of home-canning botulism and home-canned vegetables the most common cause of US outbreaks; pressure canning is the only recommended method for low-acid foods; do not use a boiling water canner or an electric multi-cooker for them; use a canner that holds at least four 1-quart jars upright, an accurate gauge (county extension offices often check gauges), vented before pressurizing; use current processing times for old recipes; can only a year's worth; store 50 to 70 F for quality, never above 95 F; boil home-canned low-acid foods and tomatoes 10 minutes plus 1 minute per additional 1,000 ft before eating; signs of contamination; if in doubt, throw it out.
source.notes: Page lists 'Published May 15, 2024' and 'Updated April 25, 2024', which is the order CDC shows; recorded as shown.

source.title: Guide 1: Principles of Home Canning (USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning, rev. 2015)
source.publisher: USDA National Institute of Food and Agriculture, hosted by NCHFP
source.supports: Storage of canned food (clean, cool, dark, dry; not above 95 F or near heat sources or in direct sunlight); accidental freezing does not by itself cause spoilage unless jars unseal; identifying spoilage (check seals, bubbles, odors, spurting liquid, mold); spoiled low-acid foods may show little evidence and should be treated as having produced botulinum toxin, with sealed suspects double-bagged for the trash and unsealed ones detoxified before disposal; contact with the toxin can be fatal whether ingested or through the skin.
source.notes: A 40-page PDF. READ SCOPE: the extracted text was searched and read only in these sections: 'Ensuring safe canned foods' (incl. the 95 F figure), 'Equipment and methods not recommended', 'Reprocessing unsealed jars', 'Storing canned foods' and 'Identifying and handling spoiled canned food' (the cleanup paragraph was read only up to the start of the bleach-solution sentence). The rest was NOT read. Detoxification steps are not reproduced in the articles. Kind changed to regulator because the publisher is a USDA agency; it is hosted by a university.

source.title: Be Prepared for a Power Outage (FEMA V-1008)
source.supports: Keep freezers and refrigerators closed; a refrigerator keeps food cold for about 4 hours and a full freezer stays at a safe temperature for about 48 hours; do not store food outside or in snow; keep a thermometer in the refrigerator and freezer; throw away refrigerated food exposed to 40 F or higher for more than 4 hours, and food with an unusual odor, color or texture; make a plan with your doctor for refrigerating medicines and powering medical devices; replace refrigerated medications if the power is out for a day or more unless the drug's label says otherwise, call your doctor or pharmacist if you depend on refrigerated medication that has been at room temperature, and use the medicine only until you have a new supply; use generators outdoors at least 20 feet from building openings.
source.notes: READ SCOPE: the whole one-page sheet, read as text extracted with pdftotext from a local copy of the PDF fetched 2026-10-30 (Firecrawl and the web-fetch tool could not extract it; Firecrawl was out of credits). Document code and date read from the sheet itself: 'FEMA V-1008/December 2023'. This is newer than the Ready.gov Food page's 'two hours' framing, and it is the document used for the medication line. We did not read the older 2020 FEMA wording the lead mentioned.

source.title: People at Increased Risk for Food Poisoning
source.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (NCEZID)
source.supports: Higher-risk groups for severe food poisoning: people 65 and older, children under 5, people with weakened immune systems (examples listed), and pregnant women; it is especially important for them to take steps to prevent food poisoning; it points to separate 'Safer Food Choices' pages for each group.
source.notes: READ SCOPE: the whole page, read in a browser pane on 2026-10-30. One date shown (Jan. 31, 2025), not labelled published, updated or reviewed. The four 'Safer Food Choices' pages it links were NOT read, so no food-specific advice for these groups is taken from this source.

source.title: Guidelines for Personal Hygiene During an Emergency
source.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (National Center for Environmental Health)
source.supports: Handwashing with soap and water for at least 20 seconds; boiled or disinfected water for handwashing only if local authorities or a doctor recommend extra caution; a temporary handwashing station from a large water jug; alcohol-based sanitizer with at least 60% alcohol and its limits (does not eliminate all germs, may not remove chemicals, less effective on visibly dirty or greasy hands); bathing guidance and when not to bathe (sewage, toxic chemicals, flood-contaminated rivers, streams and lakes); brushing teeth with clean water; protecting wounds (Vibrio, waterproof bandage, seek care for redness, swelling or oozing); pointer to CDC diapering fact sheets.
source.notes: Page shows 'Updated: July 18, 2024' before 'Published: September 16, 2024'; both recorded as shown. Upgrades the register placeholder of the same id.

source.title: NOAA Weather Radio (NWS Cheyenne office page)
source.publisher: National Weather Service, Cheyenne, WY Weather Forecast Office
source.supports: NOAA Weather Radio All Hazards is a nationwide network broadcasting official warnings, watches, forecasts and other hazard information 24 hours a day; it works with the FCC's Emergency Alert System; a special radio is needed; useful receiver features are Tone Alert, Specific Area Message Encoding (SAME) to alert for your county only, and battery backup.
source.notes: A regional (Cheyenne) office page, kept because it is the URL listed in the register placeholder. It carries no publication or review date. The national page (health-nws-nwr-national) is the one cited for frequencies and coverage. Upgrades the register placeholder of the same id.

source.title: NOAA Weather Radio All Hazards (national program page)
source.supports: NWR is a nationwide network of radio stations broadcasting from the nearest NWS office; it also carries warnings for non-weather hazards (earthquakes, chemical releases, AMBER alerts, 911 telephone outages); more than 1,000 transmitters covering all 50 states, coastal waters, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands and U.S. Pacific territories; a special receiver or scanner is required; seven VHF frequencies (162.400 to 162.550 MHz); the page lists transmitters that are degraded or out of service and says to check county coverage listings for alternate transmitters.
source.notes: Undated page. It displays a live list of transmitter outages, so its content changes continuously. Read scope: full page as returned, including the live outage list; the linked FAQ, alert-information and receiver pages were not opened.

source.title: What to Do to Protect Yourself During a Power Outage
source.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (National Center for Environmental Health)
source.supports: Medication safety in an outage: some drugs need refrigeration to keep their strength; when the power is out for a day or more, throw away refrigerated medication unless the label says otherwise; if a life depends on a refrigerated drug that has been at room temperature, use it only until a new supply is available; replace refrigerated drugs as soon as possible. Also: safe water for drinking, cooking and hygiene is bottled, boiled or treated; carbon monoxide rules (never run a generator indoors or less than 20 feet from a window, door or vent; Poison Control 1-800-222-1222); fridge and freezer hold times.
source.notes: Page shows 'Updated: January 26, 2024' while also showing 'Reviewed: August 26, 2026'; both recorded as shown.

source.title: Guidelines for Septic and Onsite Wastewater Systems
source.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (National Center for Environmental Health)
source.supports: Emergencies can damage sewer systems and cause untreated wastewater to overflow; avoid contact with floodwater that may contain sewage; signs a septic system is not working; limit toilet flushing, dishwashing, laundry and showering during an emergency; flush toilets as little as possible or use a temporary toilet; do not pump a septic tank more than halfway after flooding; do not drink well water until it is known to be safe; have a damaged system professionally inspected.
source.notes: Written for flood and similar emergencies.

source.title: Potential Sanitation Solutions During an Emergency Response (archived)
source.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (archive.cdc.gov; NCEZID, Division of Foodborne, Waterborne, and Environmental Diseases)
source.supports: In emergencies, preventing open defecation and containing waste are critical to reducing disease spread; handwashing facilities with soap and water belong at every sanitation facility; a comparison of packet latrines, bucket latrines, chemical toilets, trench and pit latrines and ecological-sanitation toilets with their advantages and constraints (flooding, high water table, access for disabled, elderly and small children, disposal needs).
source.notes: ARCHIVED CDC page, not maintained, written for emergency response in settlements and cholera-prone areas (global WASH), not for a single household. Cited only for general principles and the options comparison, never for household quantities.

source.title: Safe Drug Use After a Natural Disaster
source.publisher: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (Center for Drug Evaluation and Research)
source.supports: Keep a current medicine list (name, strength, purpose, amount and timing, conditions, supplies, allergies) and a copy of prescriptions; know how much you have; get early refills if pharmacy access may be disrupted; ask a pharmacist or provider about an emergency supply and state emergency refill laws; watertight containers kept above flood risk; a plan to keep refrigerated medicines cold with a cooler and ice or gel packs; discard medicines that touched floodwater or unsafe water; consider replacing medicines exposed to fire heat; limited exception for lifesaving drugs; reconstitute only with purified or bottled water; for refrigerated medicines check the storage instructions or ask a pharmacist, provider or manufacturer; life-sustaining medicine may be used until a replacement is available.
source.notes: Date taken from the page's modified-time metadata (09/01/2026); the page body shows no visible date.

source.title: Information Regarding Insulin Storage and Switching Between Products in an Emergency
source.publisher: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (Center for Drug Evaluation and Research)
source.supports: Label storage for insulin in a refrigerator at about 36 F to 46 F; manufacturer vials or cartridges, opened or unopened, can be left at 59 F to 86 F for up to 28 days; diluted or decanted insulin discarded within two weeks; extreme temperatures reduce effectiveness; do not use frozen insulin; keep insulin away from heat and sun; insulin in a pump's infusion set discarded after 48 hours unless the pump's instructions differ; call the manufacturer with questions; and the page's own instruction that insulin should be switched under a doctor's care with close blood-sugar monitoring.
source.notes: The page also contains unit-conversion tables for switching between insulin products. This archive deliberately does NOT reproduce them. Date taken from page metadata (modified 09/28/2026). The page's manufacturer phone table is not reproduced either, because the page itself says the numbers change. Read scope: full page as returned, including the switching tables (not reproduced).

source.title: FDA Offers Tips about Medical Devices and Natural Disasters
source.publisher: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (Center for Devices and Radiological Health)
source.supports: Keep devices and supplies clean and dry; people who depend on a device to stay alive should seek emergency services and, if possible, ask the local public health authority about evacuation before adverse weather; tell the electric company and fire department about a device that needs power; ask the manufacturer or distributor whether a device can run on batteries or a generator; do not plug in a wet cord or device; devices often reset to a default mode when power is interrupted, so check settings when power returns; do not reuse single-use devices; clean multi-use devices only as the manufacturer directs and do not boil them unless the label allows; heat and humidity can affect glucose meters and test strips; use dry ice or instant cold packs rather than ice if water contamination is a danger; devices such as dialyzers and IV pumps need safe water; carbon monoxide warning for generators.
source.notes: SOURCE DISAGREEMENT: this page gives its own bleach-dosing figures (for 5.25% bleach, 1/8 teaspoon per gallon of clear water, 1/4 teaspoon if cloudy) that differ from the CDC table in making-water-safer (8 drops per gallon, double if cloudy). The medical-devices guide does NOT reprint either; it points to the water guide and to the device manufacturer. Reviewer to note the discrepancy for the lead.

source.title: About the HHS emPOWER Program
source.publisher: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (ASPR, with CMS)
source.supports: emPOWER, launched in 2013 by ASPR and CMS, uses Medicare claims data to give public health authorities, emergency managers and responders de-identified counts of at-risk people who rely on electricity-dependent durable medical equipment and certain essential health services (dialysis, home oxygen, home health, hospice); its data covers over 4.6 million Medicare beneficiaries; prolonged outages can put such individuals in life-threatening situations within hours or days; it is a program for partners, and the page does not tell individuals how to enrol or what to do themselves.
source.notes: The program home page and About page address public health authorities, not individual households. We found no individual self-registration instructions on either page, and do not claim there are none elsewhere.

source.title: Power Outages
source.supports: A power outage may prevent use of medical devices; have alternate plans for refrigerating medicines or powering medical devices; inventory the items that rely on electricity and plan for batteries, power banks and other alternatives; talk to your medical provider about an outage plan for powered devices and refrigerated medicines, ask how long a medication can be stored at higher temperatures, and get specific guidance for life-critical medications; if power is out for more than a day, discard refrigerated medication unless the label says otherwise and consult a doctor or pharmacist for a new supply; generator and carbon monoxide rules (outdoors, at least 20 feet from windows, doors and attached garages).
source.notes: Read scope: full page as returned; linked PDFs not opened except the December 2023 fact sheet, which is registered separately (health-fema-power-outage-sheet).

source.title: People with Disabilities
source.supports: Support network; many city and county emergency management agencies keep voluntary registries for people with disabilities; know more than one dialysis or treatment facility; ask the power provider for priority power restoration; organize prescriptions; medical alert tags; list of device styles and serial numbers; backup oxygen; spare batteries and a manual backup for a power wheelchair; keep model information and where equipment came from; weather radio with text display and flashing alert for people who are deaf or hard of hearing; extra hearing-aid batteries; FEMA App alerts for up to five locations; several days' supply of prescription medicines.
source.notes: Read scope: full page as returned; linked PDFs and videos were not opened.

source.title: Build A Kit
source.supports: Basic kit items include water (one gallon per person per day for several days, for drinking and sanitation), a battery-powered or hand-crank radio and a NOAA Weather Radio with tone alert, flashlight, extra batteries, whistle, moist towelettes, garbage bags and plastic ties for personal sanitation, local maps, and a cell phone with chargers and a backup battery; additional items include soap, hand sanitizer, prescription medications, feminine supplies, diapers and wipes, and personal hygiene items.
source.notes: Read scope: full page as returned; the linked printable checklist PDF was not opened.

source.title: Make A Plan
source.supports: Plan around five questions, the first being how you will receive emergency alerts and warnings; know how you will contact one another and reconnect if separated; pick a familiar, easy-to-find family meeting place; account for medical needs including prescriptions and equipment, disabilities and access needs, languages, pets and service animals; document and practice the plan.
source.notes: Read scope: full page as returned; the fillable plan form and linked PDFs were not opened.

source.title: Emergency Alerts
source.supports: Wireless Emergency Alerts (short alerts to WEA-enabled phones in a locally targeted area; unique sound and vibration; not affected by network congestion; no charge, no subscription; older phones may not be capable and some phones require WEA to be enabled; some carriers call them Government Alerts or Emergency Alert Messages); the Emergency Alert System (broadcast TV and radio, satellite audio, cable); NOAA Weather Radio All Hazards; IPAWS (FEMA does not review, edit or approve alerts); the FEMA App (NWS alerts for up to five locations, shelter finder).
source.notes: Read scope: full page as returned; linked PDFs (WEA fact sheet, guide for alerts and warnings) were not opened.

source.title: Integrated Public Alert & Warning System
source.supports: IPAWS is FEMA's national system for local alerting; alerts are authenticated and delivered through multiple pathways at once (Emergency Alert System via AM, FM and satellite radio and broadcast, cable and satellite TV; Wireless Emergency Alerts to phones by location, 'even if cellular networks are overloaded'; NOAA Weather Radio; internet services; sirens and digital road signs); more than 2,000 federal, state, local, tribal and territorial alerting authorities use it; multiple pathways increase the likelihood a message reaches the public.
source.notes: Read scope: full page as returned; linked fact sheets, myths-and-facts and FAQ pages were not opened.

source.title: Wireless Emergency Alerts
source.supports: WEA delivers warnings to wireless devices; wireless provider participation is voluntary but participating providers must meet FCC requirements; alerts are sent by authorized officials through IPAWS to providers and pushed from cell towers to devices in the affected area; WEA and the Emergency Alert System are the two main components of the national public warning system; the page lists a 2023 FCC item seeking partners to test delivering alerts during cell tower outages (the item itself was not read).
source.notes: The FCC page's own robots metadata is 'noindex'; the content is nonetheless live on fcc.gov. Read scope: the explanatory text and resources list; the long releases archive (2007-2026 rulemaking and waiver titles) was scanned for titles only, and no archive item was opened.

source.title: Tips for Communicating in an Emergency
source.supports: Emergencies create network congestion; limit non-emergency calls and keep calls brief; try text messaging, which may go through when a call will not; try several services (text, email, landline); wait 10 seconds before redialing; have charged batteries and car-charger adapters; keep emergency numbers in the phone; place calls while the vehicle is stationary; have a family communications plan with an out-of-area central contact; forward a home number to a wireless number when evacuating; keep a corded phone that does not depend on electricity; for people with disabilities, medical alert systems usually need a working phone line so keep a backup.
source.notes: Undated; some wording (pagers, PDAs, text radio) reflects older technology. Cited for its congestion advice, which it states generally.

source.title: Toilet Use During an Emergency
source.supports: When a toilet will not flush: use a working toilet elsewhere, or turn off the toilet's water valve, flush out the bowl, line it with a plastic kitchen garbage bag inside another, add an absorbent such as kitty litter, peat moss or lime, tie the inner bag when full, store used bags away from children, pets and wildlife, and wash hands with soap and running water (wipes and sanitizer if there is none); a five-gallon bucket with a seat works the same way; a 'cat hole' only if nothing else is possible and only for a day or two, on dry land at least 100 feet from wells, homes and open water, at least 6 inches deep and about 6 inches across, one use per hole; non-biodegradable items go in a bag in the garbage.
source.notes: SOURCE DISAGREEMENT with health-osu-sanitation on disposal: this page says bagged waste can be put in the garbage can for disposal; the OSU Extension guide says human waste should not go in the normal garbage or landfill and should be stored until the public sanitary system is repaired. Our article tells readers to follow local authority instructions and flags the conflict. Read scope: full page as returned; linked county brochures not opened.

source.title: Survival Basics: Sanitation and Waste Management (EM 9334)
source.publisher: Oregon State University Extension Service (Kraemer, Hyde and Black)
source.supports: Twin-bucket (separate urine and feces) emergency toilet: two 5-gallon buckets, heavy-duty 13-gallon bags of 3 to 5 mil for the feces bucket, about a half cup of carbon material (sawdust, wood shavings, shredded paper, bark chips or peat moss) after each use, fill the feces bucket no more than half full, double-bag and store waste away from food, water, pets and pests; dilute and pour urine on ground, changing location, and do not bury waste within 100 feet of a water source; do not put human waste in the normal garbage; handwashing station of a potable-water jug with spigot, soap, towels and a catch bucket, two stations if possible; hand sanitizer limits; turn off household water and avoid using toilets even if your own pipes seem fine, because street pipes may be broken; diapers, menstrual products and mobility considerations; supplies list.
source.notes: Peer reviewed (Gray level per OSU). Written for the Pacific Northwest earthquake scenario but framed for any loss of water and sewer. Page metadata gives published 2021-10-14 and modified 2025-09-24; the visible date is October 2021. Read scope: full page as returned; the linked RDPO toilet guidebook, PHLUSH documents and the PDF edition were not opened.

source.title: Be Prepared for a Power Outage (FEMA V-1008, December 2023)
source.supports: One-page FEMA fact sheet: make a plan for refrigerating medicines and powering medical devices; talk to your doctor about how you will use electrically powered devices and store medications; 'Replace refrigerated medications if the power is out for a day or more, unless the drug's label says otherwise. Call your doctor or pharmacist if you depend on refrigerated medications that have been at room temperature. Only use the medicine until you have a new supply.'; generators outdoors at least 20 feet from building openings; learn the signs of carbon monoxide poisoning.
source.notes: READ IN FULL: one page; text extracted with pdftotext from the saved PDF bytes (the first fetch tool could not decode it). Printed edition 'FEMA V-1008/December 2023'; exact day not printed, so 2023-12-01 is a placeholder for the month. File metadata shows last modified 2023-12-29. Wording says 'Replace', whereas the Ready.gov power-outage web page (updated 2026-06-04, health-ready-power-outages) says 'discard'; both are shown in medication-and-devices.

source.title: The prairie traveler. A hand-book for overland expeditions (Randolph B. Marcy), Harper & Brothers, 1861 printing
source.publisher: Library of Congress (Joseph Meredith Toner Collection, digitized book)
source.supports: Digitized public-domain handbook by Capt. Randolph B. Marcy, U.S. Army, 'published by authority of the War Department'. Contents list (seven chapters, read in full) shows chapters on routes, wagons and teams, stores and provisions (including anti-scorbutics), camp life including fuel and making fires, and guides. Preface says it draws on the author's frontier experience and on officers' reports for the routes.
source.notes: Upgraded from the register placeholder. The drafting agent read the LOC catalogue record and the OCR snippets of the first 25 of 398 page images (title page, copyright page, preface, both contents pages and the opening of chapter I). The two contents pages (images 17 and 18) were read in full on 2026-11-01; the book's full-text file could not be fetched (404), NOT the body chapters. No passage from the chapters is quoted or relied on. The LOC copy is the 1861 printing; the title page shows a copyright entry of 1860, and the work postdates the 1846-47 events discussed in pioneer-supply-chains-failed. Rights: LOC says books in this collection are in the public domain.

source.title: Trails to Utah and the Pacific diaries and letters, 1846-1869 (Library of Congress American Memory collection)
source.publisher: Library of Congress, with Harold B. Lee Library (Brigham Young University) and the Utah Academic Library Consortium
source.supports: Catalogue record for a digitized collection of 49 diaries, 43 maps, 82 photographs and illustrations, and seven published guides for emigrants, about Mormon and other pioneers moving west to Utah, Montana and the Pacific between 1847 and 1869 (collection title runs from 1846).
source.notes: Upgraded from the register placeholder; the placeholder title 'Pioneer diaries collection' was not the record's actual title. The drafting agent read the catalogue record only, NOT the diaries. The collection is mostly Latter Day Saint migration to Utah and is not a Donner Party source; it is cited only as a place to read ordinary overland provisioning in the travelers' own words.

source.title: Ways of Catching a Spark: A History of Fire-Making Methods
source.supports: Museum overview of fire-making: tinder is a fine material that combusts easily; methods fall into percussion, friction, compression of air, chemical, solar and electrical; flint-and-steel is among the oldest and most widespread; friction methods need great skill, fitness and knowledge of conditions; fire pistons (patented in France and England in 1807); Dobereiner's lamp (1823); sulphur splints from China c. 577 AD; John Walker's friction match 1826 (sulfur, antimony sulfide, potassium chlorate, gum; drawn over sandpaper; flaming balls sometimes fell off); white phosphorus (Charles Sauria, 1830) and 'phossy jaw'; 1888 Matchgirl Strikes at Bryant and May; safety matches pioneered by Gustaf Erik Pasch in 1844; ferrocerium (1903) and the lighter.
source.notes: The page itself says most objects in the collection were acquired by a collector in the late 19th and early 20th centuries and that tracing provenance is difficult and part of a problematic colonial tradition; we repeat that caveat. Dates for the earliest methods are given by the museum as unclear. No image from this page is used.

source.title: John Walker's Friction Light (A History of the World, object contributed by Preston Hall Museum and Park)
source.publisher: BBC / British Museum 'A History of the World' project; object contributed by Preston Hall Museum and Park (Stockton Museum Service)
source.supports: Museum-contributed record of an original friction match (wood, about 9 cm by 0.5 cm). Says Walker, a Stockton-on-Tees chemist, found in 1826 that a chemical-coated stick ignited when scraped on his hearth; first sold on 12 April 1827; early matches were cardboard, then hand-cut wooden splints, later boxed with sandpaper; Walker was advised to patent but did not; Samuel Jones of London launched 'Lucifers' in 1829.
source.notes: ARCHIVED page ('no longer updated'); content is written by the contributing museum, not the BBC. DISAGREES with Tees Valley Museums on the first sale date (12 April vs 7 April 1827); see hist-field-tvm-walker. Image on the page is credited to Stockton Museum Service and is not used.

source.title: John Walker and the friction match
source.publisher: Tees Valley Museums (Preston Park Museum collection)
source.supports: Walker (born 1781) opened a chemist's shop in Stockton in 1819; made his first friction match by accident in 1826 when a stirring stick scraped against his hearth caught alight; sold his first box on 7 April 1827; did not patent even after advice from Michael Faraday; remained uncredited for decades; a sculpture was unveiled in Stockton in 1977; an original Walker match is in the Preston Park Museum collection.
source.notes: DISAGREES with the BBC-hosted museum record on the first sale date (7 April vs 12 April 1827). Museum blog post, written by the museum service; used with attribution. Images on the page are credited to Preston Park Museum and are not used.

source.title: Flint and Steel (Pipe Spring National Monument mystery objects)
source.publisher: U.S. National Park Service, Pipe Spring National Monument
source.supports: Park interpretive page: before matches, flint and steel were used for fire; striking steel across flint or other quartz chips off tiny flakes of metal that the action heats until they catch fire; most people carried char cloth, a cloth charred in a fire and smothered, which the sparks ignite and which is then transferred to a tinder bundle and blown into flame; both pioneers and American Indians used flint and steel; steel was a popular trade item.
source.notes: Short, undated-author interpretive text, last updated 2015. Gives no accuracy or reliability figures. We use it only to describe what the tools were, not as instruction.

source.title: tinder box (iron), object record DL.376794
source.publisher: Smithsonian National Museum of American History
source.supports: Collection record for an iron tinder box classified by the Smithsonian as 'Fire-making and controlling equipment', related to 'Home and Community Life: Domestic Life'; not on view.
source.notes: Very sparse record: no date, maker, or use description. Cited only to show that tinder boxes are in the national collection under domestic life. The Smithsonian says its database is a work in progress. No image used.

source.title: Outdoor Fire Safety
source.supports: Unintentional actions are the leading cause of outside fires; use propane, charcoal and wood-pellet grills only outside (indoor use can cause fire or carbon monoxide poisoning); build campfires at least 25 feet from tents, shrubs and anything that can burn; fire pits, chimneys and outdoor fireplaces at least 10 feet from the home or anything that can burn; watch children at fire pits; use a metal screen over wood-burning fires; put fires out before leaving; store matches and lighters out of children's sight and reach.
source.notes: Read in full (short page). DISCREPANCY: campfire distance is 25 ft here, 15 ft at NPS, and 10 ft for fire pits at NFPA (NFPA 1 fire code: 50 ft for open fires where adopted, per NFPA's summary). The article reports the range and defers to the local fire authority.

source.title: Campfires
source.supports: Know the local rules and fire conditions (windy and dry weather may mean campfires are banned) and ask the park before you go; keep tents and flammables at least 15 feet away and upwind; use matches or a lighter on a firestarter; use only lighter fluid as an accelerant and never gasoline; never leave a campfire unattended and keep water nearby; burning anything but wood, especially plastics, can produce toxic gases; douse with plenty of water, and in a pinch stir sand or dirt into spread-out coals; if a fire gets out of control, note your location and call 911.
source.notes: Read in full. Page last updated 2017-04-17, the oldest of the fire-safety sources. It permits lighter fluid where the park allows; the NFPA article says never to use gasoline or other flammable or combustible liquids. The article follows the stricter statement and names the difference.

source.title: Wildfire Prevention Tips for Fire Pits and Outdoor Fires (Michele Steinberg, NFPA)
source.publisher: National Fire Protection Association (nonprofit fire-code and standards developer)
source.supports: Contact the local fire department about requirements and restrictions before any outdoor fire; some places never allow outdoor fire, others restrict it by season or conditions; avoid burning anything outdoors on windy, dry days because embers can ignite structures or cause a wildfire; supervise outdoor fires; never burn plastics, treated lumber, tires, paint or aerosol containers; never use gasoline or other flammable liquids; fire pits at least 10 feet from anything that can burn; NFPA 1 (where adopted) requires permits and 50 feet from structures for outdoor fires, and an attendant with extinguishing equipment.
source.notes: NFPA staff article summarizing NFPA educational messages and the NFPA 1 fire code; the article says its opinions are the author's. The drafting agent read the whole article, NOT the NFPA 1 code itself, so the 50-foot and permit statements are reported as NFPA's summary of the code. Kind corrected to 'nonprofit' after the lead's validator change.

source.title: Carbon Monoxide (CO) Poisoning Basics
source.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (National Center for Environmental Health)
source.supports: CO is an odorless, colorless gas that kills without warning; produced when fuel burns in vehicles, small engines, stoves, lanterns, grills, fireplaces, gas ranges and furnaces; symptoms are headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain and confusion, often described as flu-like; people who are sleeping or intoxicated can die before symptoms; never burn charcoal indoors; never use a portable gas camp stove indoors; do not cook or burn anything in a stove or fireplace that is not vented; install battery-operated or battery backup CO detectors near every sleeping area; operate generators only outdoors more than 20 feet from windows, doors and vents.
source.notes: Page was re-dated 2026-10-26, three days before verification. Generator and vehicle-exhaust practices are not reproduced in the article; it links out.

source.title: Prepare! Don't Let a Winter Storm Take You by Surprise
source.supports: For winter travel: avoid traveling alone; tell someone your timetable and primary and alternate routes; call 511 for road and weather conditions and restrictions before leaving; carry a Winter Storm Survival Kit whose list includes blankets or sleeping bags, high-calorie non-perishable food, a candle and matches (for light and, in an emergency, heat), a small can and waterproof matches to melt snow, and a compass and road maps, 'don't depend on mobile devices with limited battery life'; more than 5,000 people are killed on average each year in weather-related vehicle crashes.
source.notes: Page carries no visible update date (page metadata shows 2019 creation). Only the travel-planning and kit-contents statements are used; no quantities are reproduced.

source.title: What To Do If You're Caught in a Winter Storm
source.supports: In a vehicle: let someone know where you are going and what route you will take so a search can start in the right place; if the car is stuck, stay in the vehicle because leaving means becoming disoriented quickly in wind-driven snow and cold; be visible to rescuers. The page also gives engine-running and exhaust-pipe instructions to avoid carbon monoxide poisoning, which this archive does not reproduce.
source.notes: Page carries no visible update date (metadata shows 2019). Contains engine-running timing and a statement that outdoors with no shelter one should 'build a fire for heat'; neither is reproduced or endorsed by this archive. Flagged for the safety reviewer of fire-making-across-time.

source.title: What made the search for longitude so important?
source.supports: Navigational errors and long voyages killed crews; on 22 October 1707 five of Admiral Sir Cloudesley Shovell's ships struck the Isles of Scilly, four sank and more than 1,400 men died, with navigational errors the cause; Spain offered the first longitude reward in 1567 and other states followed; Galileo proposed Jupiter's moons in 1610 and Newton later noted that telescope length and a ship's motion made those eclipses impossible to observe at sea; Longitude Act of 9 July 1714 offered a public reward of 20,000 pounds.
source.notes: RMG notes there is no evidence of a public outcry after 1707 and that the Act seems to have resulted from lobbying by mathematicians. We keep that nuance.

source.title: Longitude found - the story of Harrison's timekeepers
source.supports: Harrison's H1 (1735) trialled on a 1736 voyage to Lisbon; H4 trialled to Jamaica in 1761 and in the 1763-64 Barbados trial alongside lunar and Jupiter-satellite methods; in February 1765 the Board of Longitude found H4 kept time within the most stringent limits of the 1714 Act, but held back the remainder of the reward until other makers could build similar timekeepers; further testing at the Royal Observatory from 1766 went poorly and the dispute rekindled; marine chronometers were initially very expensive, so roll-out was slow, and cheaper simplified designs allowed wider take-up in the early 1800s.
source.notes: RMG states that the Harrison family felt the Commissioners had changed the rules; we report both sides as RMG does.

source.title: Longitude found: Nevil Maskelyne and the lunar method
source.supports: Tobias Mayer's lunar tables with a good instrument could, per James Bradley, give a ship's longitude to within 1 degree; the instrument refined in sea trials became the first marine sextant (John Bird); on the 1761 voyage to St Helena Maskelyne found lunars only 1.5 degrees in error against errors of up to 10 degrees from dead reckoning; the calculations were 'decidedly lengthy'; the Nautical Almanac was created to pre-compute lunar data, much of it processed by assistants (computers); marine timekeepers remained rare and expensive; dead reckoning was not abandoned and navigators might use all methods.
source.notes: These are figures from a single 1761 trial as RMG reports them; they are not a general accuracy claim for later practice.

source.title: Sextant (Jesse Ramsden, last quarter of the 18th century), Time and Navigation exhibition
source.publisher: Smithsonian Institution (National Museum of American History object; Time and Navigation exhibition, National Air and Space Museum)
source.supports: Exhibition record for a sextant made by Jesse Ramsden in the last quarter of the 18th century; the sextant became the symbol of navigation; the instrument is named for its scale of 60 degrees, one sixth of a circle, and can measure larger angles than the octant.
source.notes: Short caption-level record. No image used (Smithsonian credit lines apply).

source.title: What is declination?
source.supports: At most places a compass does not point exactly to geographic north; the deviation is called declination; it has been a nuisance to navigators for centuries and varies with both location and time; at very high latitudes a compass can even point south; the collar of USGS topographic maps shows the magnetic declination at the map center in the year the map was made; NOAA offers a calculator for any location and date.
source.notes: Page was fetched in full; the output was large and only the explanatory text was read.

source.title: What do the different north arrows on a USGS topographic map mean?
source.supports: A diagram at the bottom of most USGS topographic maps shows true north, grid north and magnetic north and the angles between them; some maps, especially very old ones, do not have it; true north is the direction of the line of longitude bisecting the quadrangle; magnetic north on the map is the direction a magnetic compass would point at the time the map was published, and it varies over time and with position.
source.notes: Only the opening explanation was read closely; the rest of the large page (related links) was skimmed.

source.title: Magnetic Declination
source.publisher: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information
source.supports: Declination is the angle between magnetic north and true north, positive east and negative west; it changes over time and with location; a compass points along the horizontal component of the local magnetic field, not at any single point such as the magnetic pole; true bearing is magnetic bearing plus declination when west is negative; NOAA provides calculators and the World Magnetic Model.
source.notes: Does not state the size of declination anywhere in the US; we do not either.

source.title: What is the North Star and How Do You Find It?
source.publisher: NASA Science (Preston Dyches, public engagement specialist)
source.supports: Polaris is not the brightest star but is usually easy to spot; it sits close to, not exactly at, the north celestial pole and traces a very small circle, so it stays in roughly the same place and is a reliable way to find the direction of north in the Northern Hemisphere (true north, not magnetic); the two pointer stars at the end of the Big Dipper's cup point to Polaris; the Southern Hemisphere has no bright star marking the south celestial pole and observers there can use other ways, including the Southern Cross; the pole star changes over thousands of years because of a roughly 26,000-year wobble.
source.notes: The page gives no numerical accuracy for using Polaris as a direction guide. We state none.

source.title: Donner and Reed Wagon Train Incident
source.publisher: U.S. National Park Service, California National Historic Trail
source.supports: Lansford W. Hastings claimed a timesaving route (the Hastings Cutoff) through the Great Salt Lake Desert; late starters found it enticing; the Donner-Reed party of 87 people left Illinois on April 12 and passed Independence, Missouri on May 12 with 2,500 miles to go, joining Hastings' group of 80 wagons to save 150-500 miles (Hastings 'a little vague'); the route took more time than the popular routes, depleting supplies and livestock; they reached the Humboldt River on September 26 and Truckee Lake in October, exhausted and low on provisions, and were trapped by snow for four months; once the animals were killed by mid-December they ate rawhide; some left on a self-rescue mission and resorted to cannibalism; 40 of the 87 died of starvation-related causes; survivors were not rescued until spring 1847. Quotes Sarah Winnemucca that her Paiute people 'would have helped' but were afraid.
source.notes: DISCREPANCIES with other sources: NPS counts 87 people and 40 deaths; McCurdy (1994) counts 90 people and 42 deaths; Britannica says Donners and Reeds left Springfield April 14 and gives 42 deaths and 47 survivors; the Utah state history essay says 47 of 87 reached Sutter's Fort. The NPS page also gives the departure from Illinois as April 12. The saving Hastings claimed is stated as 150-500 miles by NPS and 'more than 300 miles' by Britannica. Read in full (short page). Kind 'museum' is the closest fit for an NPS interpretive history page; flagged.

source.title: The Hastings Cutoff (Thomas G. Alexander, from Utah, The Right Place)
source.publisher: Utah Division of State History (History to Go)
source.supports: Hastings published his Emigrants Guide to Oregon and California in 1845; it is unclear whether he meant to promote the cutoff from Fort Bridger or only to say that a more direct route than via Fort Hall was possible; Fremont, Hudspeth, Bridger and Vasquez favored the cutoff, while James Clyman tried to dissuade the Donner-Reed party and Joseph R. Walker thought it an unproven risk; four parties took the cutoff in 1846; the Donner-Reed party left Fort Bridger on July 31, found a note from Hastings warning against Weber Canyon and promising a better road, and took the Emigration Canyon route, losing more time and meeting extreme hardship there and in the Salt Lake Desert; 'only forty-seven of the original eighty-seven reached Sutter's Fort'.
source.notes: A state-agency history essay by a professional historian; short and without footnotes. Its '47 of 87' implies 40 deaths, matching NPS but not McCurdy or Britannica.

source.title: Epidemiology of disaster. The Donner Party (1846-1847) (S A McCurdy), Western Journal of Medicine 160(4):338-342
source.publisher: Western Journal of Medicine, via PubMed Central (author at UC Davis School of Medicine)
source.supports: Abstract: the party consisted of 90 persons, median age 19.5 years (range 1 to 70), 55 (61%) male, 72 (80%) traveling with family; 42 (47%) died; age was the most important mortality risk factor, with lowest mortality (10%) at ages 6 to 14 and highest for children under 6 and adults 35 and over; persons traveling without family had about twice the relative risk, as did men and boys; the author suggests that keeping family structures intact may improve survival in nutritionally stressed populations.
source.notes: The drafting agent read the abstract and bibliographic record only; the full text is scanned page images and was NOT read. The 90-person count differs from NPS and Utah's 87; the abstract does not explain the difference. A commentary, 'Previous Donner Party research', exists in volume 161, p. 92, and was not read.

source.title: Donner Memorial State Park
source.supports: The park's Visitor Center has exhibits on the Emigrant Experience, the Donner Party, the Land of the Washoe, Chinese construction of the railroad, and early motoring over Donner Pass; the Pioneer Monument, completed June 6, 1918 by the Native Sons of the Golden West (California Historical Landmark #134), stands on a 22-foot pedestal where the Schallenberger and later the Breen cabin once stood; restored in 2022; park lies near an elevation of about 6,000 feet; the park contains the alignment of the primary Emigrant Trail in Coldstream Canyon.
source.notes: A visitor-information page, not a history narrative: it gives no account of the party's deaths or supplies. Used only for the memorial, the location, and the fact that interpretation covers Indigenous peoples of the area. The plaque wording often quoted online was NOT verified here and is not used.

source.title: Donner party (Encyclopaedia Britannica)
source.publisher: Encyclopaedia Britannica (editors; most recently revised by Michael Ray)
source.supports: Tertiary reference summary: Hastings Cutoff was proposed by an unreliable guide and was in reality 125 miles longer than the established trail; Reed was warned at Fort Laramie by a friend who had just come east through the cutoff; the party spent about two weeks breaking a trail through the Wasatch; a note from Hastings said the Great Salt Lake Desert could be crossed in two days but it took five; dozens of cattle were lost and several wagons abandoned; Paiute warriors killed several remaining oxen; they cached nearly all personal possessions except food, clothing and essentials; snow blocked the pass on October 31; many oxen wandered off and were lost in the snow; deaths totaled 42 with 47 survivors; Breen's diary is the only contemporary written record of the ordeal; in 2010 researchers reported no physical evidence of cannibalism at Alder Creek while noting absence of evidence does not rule it out.
source.notes: Tertiary encyclopedia article; the register's kind list has no 'reference' kind, so 'scholarship' is the closest available and is imperfect (flagged for the lead). Read in full. Used for specific figures that NPS and the Utah essay do not give (the desert crossing, the 125-mile figure, relief-party dates), each attributed by name in the text. Its figure of 42 deaths with 47 survivors does not add up to the 87-person party it names. Britannica attributes oxen losses to Paiute warriors, whereas NPS quotes Sarah Winnemucca that her people were afraid and would have helped; the article reports the disagreement.

source.title: Patrick Breen Diary, 1846 November 20 - 1847 March 1 (BANC MSS C-E 176), finding aid
source.publisher: The Bancroft Library, University of California, Berkeley, via the Online Archive of California
source.supports: Finding aid for the manuscript diary kept by Patrick Breen at Donner (Truckee) Lake from November 20, 1846 to March 1, 1847: a 32-page booklet with entries on the first 29 pages; terse, matter-of-fact style recording weather, health, food, deaths and visits; ends on the day Reed's relief party arrived; the diary passed from Breen to George McKinstry to H. H. Bancroft; early printed versions (from a May 1847 newspaper copy) are considered corrupt through omissions, alterations or falsification; Teggart (1910) is the first complete scholarly edition and Stewart (1946) added a transcription and facsimile.
source.notes: Read in full (finding aid prose). The diary's own entries, the digital images and the container-listing transcription were NOT read. The finding aid's background paragraph repeats the standard account (starvation; some survivors consumed the dead) without citing sources. It does not say this is the only contemporary record. Finding aid dated 1997 (source date March 2011).
