source.title: The emigrants' guide to Oregon and California (Lansford W. Hastings, Cincinnati, 1845), Internet Archive scan, full text
source.publisher: Internet Archive (scan of the 1845 Cincinnati edition; holding library not verified)
source.supports: Primary source. In the passages read (OCR of printed pages around 137-139): the distance from Independence to Oregon or California by the Fort Hall route is about 2,100 miles and the usual time about 120 days exclusive of delays, though parties had often taken longer; Fort Hall is the only settlement in that vicinity where emigrants can obtain horses and provisions; a California route is described leaving the Oregon route and heading southwest toward the Salt Lake.
source.notes: The drafting agent fetched the full OCR text (about 540,000 characters) but READ ONLY the passages around the California-route summary (printed pp. ~137-139) and the Bear River valley passage; the rest was not read. The OCR is noisy and the Salt Lake passage is too garbled to quote or characterize with confidence, so no claim is made about what the guide recommends for the cutoff. The details page (archive.org/details/GR_1815) was not itself opened; the URL came from a search result and the text from /stream/GR_1815/GR_1815_djvu.txt. Other copies exist (BYU Trail Guides, HathiTrust) and were not checked.

source.title: How To Make Salt
source.publisher: National Park Service (Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail, 'Pivotal Places')
source.supports: Field, Bratton and Gibson made salt near a Clatsop-Nehalem village on the Oregon coast in winter 1805-1806; equipment named (five kettles, wood, rocks, iron kegs, seawater); NPS says almost a gallon a day working around the clock; Lewis's 'very tedious opperation' and mid-February stock of about 20 gallons with 12 secured in two kegs; Clark's remark that the salt was not so strong as rock salt.
source.notes: Interpretive article, not a research paper. NPS says 'almost a gallon of salt a day'; the journals say 3 quarts to a gallon a day (5 Jan 1806). Extent read: full page text (single short article), live scrape.

source.title: Salt Works, Oregon
source.publisher: National Park Service (Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail / Lewis and Clark National Historical Park)
source.supports: The party ran out of salt and chose to winter near the ocean to make it; salt valued for preserving meat; the three salt makers befriended people of the Clatsop-Nehalem village, who sold them whale blubber; about twenty gallons made by Lewis's count; the site is a replica salt works in Seaside, Oregon.
source.notes: NPS says Clark did not mind going without salt while Lewis found unsalted food bland; the journals confirm the contrast (5 Jan 1806). Extent read: full page text, live scrape.

source.title: December 28, 1805 (Journals of the Lewis and Clark Expedition)
source.publisher: University of Nebraska-Lincoln (Gary E. Moulton, ed., Center for Digital Research in the Humanities)
source.supports: Clark's entry detailing Joseph Field, Bratton and Gibson to form a camp at the ocean and 'Commence makeing Salt with 5 of the largest Kittles', with Willard and Wiser carrying kettles; Ordway and Whitehouse entries; editorial note that the camp was at present Seaside, ran until 21 February 1806 and produced about three or four bushels; editorial note on Clatsop winter villages at Seaside.
source.notes: The editors' footnote (three or four bushels) and the NPS gallon figures are different units and are not reconciled by any source we read. Extent read: the whole page (Clark x2, Ordway, Whitehouse entries and editors' footnotes 1-5), live scrape. No other journal dates were read except 5 Jan and 21 Feb 1806.

source.title: January 5, 1806 (Journals of the Lewis and Clark Expedition)
source.publisher: University of Nebraska-Lincoln (Gary E. Moulton, ed., Center for Digital Research in the Humanities)
source.supports: Lewis and Clark on the first salt delivered by Willard and Wiser: camp on the coast about 15 miles from the fort near Killamuck (Lewis) / Clat Sop and Kil a mox (Clark) families; salt makers got from 3 quarts to a gallon a day; a gallon specimen; Lewis 'excellent, fine, strong, & white'; Clark 'not So Strong as the rock Salt'; no salt since 20 December; whale blubber from the Indians; Ordway and Whitehouse accounts.
source.notes: Lewis and Clark's descriptions of the salt differ in wording; Lewis names the neighbours Killamuck (Tillamook), Clark names Clatsop and Killamuck. Extent read: the whole page (Lewis, Clark, Ordway, Gass, Whitehouse entries and footnotes), live scrape.

source.title: February 21, 1806 (Journals of the Lewis and Clark Expedition)
source.publisher: University of Nebraska-Lincoln (Gary E. Moulton, ed., Center for Digital Research in the Humanities)
source.supports: The salt camp evacuated; the party returned with the salt and utensils; Lewis: stock of salt now about 20 gallons, 12 secured in 2 small iron-bound kegs for the voyage; Ordway's account of the wet return to the fort; Gass and Whitehouse accounts.
source.notes: NPS and the Lewis journal agree on 20 and 12 gallons. The editors date the end of the camp 21 February; the 1955 plaque quoted by another site says 20 February. Extent read: the whole page (Lewis, Clark, Ordway, Gass, Whitehouse entries and footnotes), live scrape.

source.title: The Salt Works (Discover Lewis & Clark)
source.supports: Secondary account of the salt works: why the camp was on the coast rather than the Netul River; five days to find a site; the oven reassembled as a 'cairn' in the 1950s; plaque text crediting the site to the testimony of Jenny Michel, whose Clatsop father pointed it out; the plaque's 'approximately four bushels' and end date.
source.notes: Public-service educational site run by the Lewis and Clark Trail Alliance; kind 'nonprofit' is the closest fit (nonprofit status not confirmed from the page). Its figures of 28 gallons produced and about 1,400 gallons of seawater are not sourced on the page and are not used as fact in our article. Extent read: full page text, live scrape.

source.title: History & Culture: People: Tribes (Lewis and Clark National Historical Park)
source.supports: The Clatsop lived on the south side of the Columbia and down the coast to Tillamook Head; the Nehalem are described as the northernmost band of the Tillamook, from Tillamook Head south to Kilchis Point; the Chinook lived on the north bank; the captains described friendly relations; Coboway received the fort; the page names the Clatsop-Nehalem Confederated Tribes and the Chinook Nation as homeland tribes.
source.notes: Read through a search result excerpt that reproduced the full page text, then not re-fetched; flagged for a human link check. Extent read: the full page text as reproduced in a search-result excerpt; the live page was not separately scraped.

source.title: Hardtack during the Civil War
source.publisher: National Park Service, Manassas National Battlefield Park (youth page)
source.supports: Civil War hardtack was made from flour, water and salt; soldiers' nicknames ('sheet iron crackers', 'tooth duller', 'worm castles'); it got wet and moldy in shipping boxes and could hold insect eggs; soldiers softened it in coffee, put it in soups, fried it; Confederates relied more on corn because wheat was less widely grown; hardtack from the war survives in the park museum.
source.notes: A youth page. It includes a home recipe with quantities, which we deliberately do not reproduce or link. Extent read: full page text, live scrape.

source.title: Cooking - Food Rations
source.publisher: National Park Service, Fort Scott National Historic Site
source.supports: U.S. Army daily ration of the 1840s (pork or salt beef, flour made into bread, beans or rice, coffee, sugar, vinegar, salt); hardtack issued on campaign and often in camp, about a pound (9-10 crackers); problems of hardness, wet, mold, maggots and weevils; the 'Hard Crackers, Come Again No More' parody; information drawn from Billings, Hardtack and Coffee.
source.notes: Page last updated 2016. Hardtack details are credited to Billings (1887) rather than to archival records. Extent read: full page text, live scrape.

source.title: Molds on Food: Are They Dangerous?
source.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
source.supports: Some molds produce mycotoxins; mold roots can run deep and invisible bacteria can grow with it; molds tolerate salt and sugar better than most invaders; handling table says to discard moldy bread and baked goods because porous foods can be contaminated below the surface; do not sniff moldy food.
source.notes: Page last updated 2013. It does not discuss ship's biscuit or hardtack; the application to dry hard bread is our reading and is labelled editor's note. Extent read: full page text, live scrape.

source.title: The prairie traveler. A hand-book for overland expeditions (full text)
source.publisher: Randolph B. Marcy; Harper & Brothers, New York (Internet Archive text of the Library of Congress copy)
source.supports: Chapter I 'Stores and Provisions': packing of bacon, pork and flour; Marcy's allowance for a grown person for 110 days (flour or its equivalent in hard bread, bacon or pork, coffee, sugar, with beef on the hoof); desiccated vegetables; antiscorbutics; 'cold flour'; his description of pemmican as the near-sole diet of the Fur Company's men; Dr Rae's 1854 daily allowance; the 1857-58 winter ration failure; the 'Jerking Meat' section.
source.notes: OCR text of the same scan (identifier prairietravelerh01marc) that the Library of Congress catalogues; OCR is noisy and quotations were checked against two readings. The LOC copy is dated 1861 (Harper, 'new edition'); the book was first published in 1859. We quote only a few words. Extent read: from the OCR of the whole book (about 535,000 characters) I read the contents list, Chapter I "Stores and Provisions" (book pp. 29-36) and the "Jerking Meat" section (pp. 160-161). The rest of the 381-page book was not read.

source.title: The prairie traveler. A hand-book for overland expeditions (Library of Congress digitized book)
source.publisher: Library of Congress (Joseph Meredith Toner Collection); Randolph B. Marcy, Harper & Brothers, 1861
source.supports: Catalogue and contents: 'published by authority of the War Department'; Chapter I contents list 'Stores and Provisions ... Pemmican ... Antiscorbutics ... Cold Flour'; Chapter V includes 'Jerking Meat'; rights statement says the book is in the public domain.
source.notes: The LOC page-level text view did not load for us; the passages we quote were read in the Internet Archive text of the same scan (see hist-food-marcy-prairie-traveler-text). Extent read: the item landing page (catalogue record, contents list and a few page-level OCR excerpts); the page-level text view did not load.

source.title: Trails to Utah and the Pacific diaries and letters, 1846-1869
source.publisher: Library of Congress (American Memory-derived collection; source material from Brigham Young University and Utah Academic Libraries Consortium)
source.supports: The collection comprises 49 diaries, 43 maps, 82 photographs and illustrations and seven published guides for emigrants, covering Mormon and other pioneers moving to Utah, Montana and the Pacific between 1847 and 1869.
source.notes: Only the collection-level description was read. We did not open individual diaries, so no diary text is quoted or paraphrased from it. The placeholder titled this 'Pioneer diaries collection'; this is the actual title. Extent read: the collection-level description only. No individual diary was opened.

source.title: Historical Origins of Food Preservation
source.publisher: National Center for Home Food Preservation, University of Georgia (Brian A. Nummer, Ph.D., May 2002)
source.supports: Overview of drying, freezing, fermenting, pickling, curing, jam and jelly, and canning; Appert's 1790s discovery and about 1806 French Navy trial; Durand's tin cans in 1810; Pasteur 1864; Chevalier-Appert's 1851 pressure retort; nitrites and C. botulinum recognised in the 1920s.
source.notes: A 2002 overview that gives some claims without citation (for example 12,000 B.C. drying, ketchup origins). We use only the dated canning, curing and refrigeration statements, and flag the rest as undocumented. Extent read: full page text, live scrape.

source.title: Jerky
source.publisher: National Center for Home Food Preservation, University of Georgia (from So Easy to Preserve, 6th ed., Bulletin 989)
source.supports: Jerky raw-meat hazards; wild game and pork trichinella treatment; heating meat strips to 160 F either in marinade before drying or in an oven after drying; fecal contamination of game; properly dried jerky keeps at room temperature two weeks in a sealed container.
source.notes: Same page as the register placeholder 'nchfp-jerky' (read at the URL without the trailing slash; both return HTTP 200). Defined under a new id because the shared test suite uses 'nchfp-jerky' as its permanent unverified-placeholder fixture. Source of an official disagreement: NCHFP allows the 160 F heat step after drying; USDA FSIS recommends it before dehydrating and says home-dried jerky keeps 1 to 2 months. See hist-food-fsis-jerky. Extent read: full page text, live scrape.

source.title: Jerky and Food Safety
source.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
source.supports: USDA Meat and Poultry Hotline's current recommendation to heat meat to 160 F and poultry to 165 F before dehydrating; explanation that dehydrators may not reach that temperature and that bacteria become more heat resistant after drying; venison fecal contamination; home-dried jerky stored 1 to 2 months, commercially packaged 12 months.
source.notes: Last updated November 2016. The old FSIS path .../meat/jerky-and-food-safety now returns 404. Extent read: the page via verbatim extraction (recommendation, reasoning, wild game and storage passages, update date) plus a search excerpt of the same page; ask.fsis.usda.gov repeats the 160 F / 165 F recommendation in a search excerpt only.

source.title: Smoking Meat and Poultry
source.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
source.supports: FSIS defines smoking as slowly cooking food indirectly over a fire and gives modern guidance for hot smoking in a purpose-built smoker: approved materials, no makeshift galvanized containers, thermometer monitoring and cooking to safe minimum internal temperatures.
source.notes: This page covers hot smoking as cooking. It does not cover cold smoking or traditional smoke-curing, and we say so on the page. Extent read: verbatim extraction of the definition, makeshift-container warning, temperature range, timing and update date, plus a search excerpt of the page. Cold smoking and curing are not mentioned in the text we saw.

source.title: Pemmican
source.publisher: The Canadian Encyclopedia (John E. Foster; updated by Daniel Baird)
source.supports: Definition (dried meat, traditionally bison, with fat, sometimes berries; Cree pimikan, 'manufactured grease'); bison-hide bags and shipping to provision voyageurs; Peter Pond credited with introducing pemmican to the trade in 1779 after obtaining it from the Chipewyans in the Athabasca region; posts on the Red, Assiniboine and North Saskatchewan Rivers acquired pemmican from Aboriginal peoples and the Metis; the 1814 Pemmican Proclamation of Governor Miles Macdonell; the Royal Navy later provisioning Arctic expeditions with beef pemmican made in England.
source.notes: Gives a proportion for the ingredients that we deliberately omit. The article's etymology (pimikan, 'manufactured grease') differs from the Metis museum document's gloss; see cluster notes. Extent read: the article text through the History section via verbatim extraction. The page has a "Recipe" section that was not read and nothing was drawn from it.

source.title: The Hudson's Bay Company Trading System (The Metis Fur Trade)
source.publisher: Virtual Museum of Metis History and Culture (metismuseum.ca); authors Patrick Young, Todd Paquin and Darren Prefontaine
source.supports: The HBC's constant need for provisions gave Metis bison hunters and pemmican provisioners their only steady market; Metis writer Alexander Ross's account of a hunt in which over 2500 animals were killed yielding 375 bags of pemmican and 240 bales of dried meat; provisioning was lucrative; pemmican prices rose sharply by the mid-1870s as few Metis lived off the hunt.
source.notes: A 42-page PDF; our extraction read only some passages, so claims are limited to those. The publisher of the virtual museum (believed to be the Gabriel Dumont Institute) was not confirmed from a page we read and is not asserted. A search excerpt of this document gives the Cree gloss 'pimmi' (fat) and 'konn' (meat); we did not confirm that wording in the PDF text. Extent read: a 42-page PDF of which only a few passages (the HBC provisioning and Ross hunt paragraphs and the title/authors) were returned by verbatim extraction, roughly one page of text in total. The rest was not read.

source.title: About The Jump! (Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump)
source.publisher: Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump World Heritage Site, Alberta, Canada
source.supports: The site's account that the Blackfoot (Siksika, Kainai/Bloods and Piikani/Peigan) pursued traditional lifeways until the buffalo's near extinction in 1881; that in fall communal kills occurred and 'the people would prepare dry meat and pemmican for winter', held as emergency supplies; Treaty No. Seven (1877).
source.notes: The site's operator and its Blackfoot partnership are not stated on the page we read; we attribute the words to the site, not to named Blackfoot authors. Extent read: the page text via verbatim extraction (history of the site, tribes, seasonal travel, Treaty 7). The linked booklet "Buffalo Tracks" was not read.

source.title: Lesson 9: How to Make Wasna
source.publisher: NATIFS (North American Traditional Indigenous Food Systems)
source.supports: NATIFS's statement that the food is known as wasna to the Lakota and Dakota people and as pemmican to Anishinaabe peoples, that Indigenous peoples across the Plains and beyond have long relied on it for hunts, seasonal travel and winter, and that many still make and share it today.
source.notes: The organisation's homepage states a mission to promote Indigenous foodways education and food access and names Chef Sean Sherman as executive director. The lesson contains a method; we neither quote nor link the method. Kind 'nonprofit' is the closest fit (nonprofit status not confirmed from the pages read). Extent read: the lesson's introductory cultural-context paragraphs only, via verbatim extraction. The method section was deliberately not read into this archive. The organisation's About page returned 404; its homepage was seen only as a search excerpt.

source.title: InterTribal Buffalo Council (Northern Plains History and Cultures)
source.publisher: Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian, Native Knowledge 360
source.supports: The bison was more than a historical food source to Northern Plains Native Nations; tribal histories, cultures, traditions and spiritual lives were connected to the buffalo in a reciprocal relationship, and people honored and cared for the bison through ceremonies and cultural protocols.
source.notes: A classroom resource for grades 9-12. Extent read: the opening paragraph only (verbatim extraction). The rest of the lesson was not read.

source.title: Preservation of Meat
source.publisher: Monticello (Thomas Jefferson Foundation), Thomas Jefferson Encyclopedia
source.supports: Enslaved workers Ursula Granger and John cut meat for hams, bacon and salt pork, covered it in salt to draw out moisture, and hung it in the smokehouse over a low-burning hardwood fire; the preserved pork, beef, mutton and fish was rationed to enslaved people, hired workers and Jefferson's household; prime cuts went to the household and less desirable cuts to enslaved workers.

source.title: Cistern Safety and Disasters: Before, During, and After

source.title: Collecting Rainwater and Your Health: An Overview

source.title: What to Do to Evacuate in a Chemical Emergency
source.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (National Center for Environmental Health)
source.supports: In some chemical emergencies staying put and sealing off the space may be dangerous and it may be safer to evacuate; follow instructions from police, fire or other local officials, who identify shelters and give directions; plan several routes; find a place that takes pets, noting that some shelters such as the American Red Cross's take only service animals; make a plan to stay in contact and expect to send messages by text or social media; go kits and medications for up to a week; check with neighbors who need a ride; call or text a friend or relative outside your area; leave a note; vehicles may not be airtight; do not go to your children, loved ones or pets unless police, fire or other local officials say it is safe, because they may be sheltered where they are; wait for the 'all clear' before returning.
source.notes: Read: the whole page as rendered by Firecrawl on 2026-11-01. human_link_check remains false.

source.title: Comprehensive School Safety Plans (California Department of Education)
source.supports: California's state education agency recommends that schools establish reunification locations and procedures and ensure parents and guardians are aware of them, and that schools inform parents in languages they understand of reunification plans and the necessity of cooperating with first responders; it also lists required safety-plan components, which this guide does not reproduce.
source.notes: Read: the whole page as rendered by Firecrawl on 2026-11-01 (about 8,000 words, mostly about school and district planning duties). The page is written for schools, districts and county offices, not parents, and is specific to California law. Page shows 'Last Reviewed: Thursday, February 5, 2026'. A banner on the page about an election is unrelated. human_link_check remains false.

source.title: Are You Ready? An In-Depth Guide to Citizen Preparedness (P-2064, September 2020)
source.supports: Fetched the full 36-page text; read the contents list and the sections cited here (introduction, protective actions, financial preparedness, Make a Plan, supplies, documents, practice schedule). The hazard-by-hazard sections were not read. Three-step frame (know your risks, make a plan, take action); first moves when something happens without warning (assess the situation, decide to stay or change location); family communication plan with an out-of-state contact reachable two ways and a wallet or digital copy for everyone; evacuation guidelines (meeting places in several directions, half-tank rule, one car per family, leave a note); basic kit contents and the 'at least 72 hours' framing; water of 1 gallon per person per day for 3, 7 or even 14 days depending on location; cash in small bills with the highest a twenty; N95 respirators; kit maintenance (first in, first out; discard swollen, dented or corroded cans; check needs every six months); critical-document storage; practice schedule and one-year timeline.
source.notes: September 2020 edition, hosted under a 2021-11 upload path. Older than the Ready.gov web pages, so where they differ the web pages are newer. Upgraded from a placeholder in register.json. The power-outage section says 'If the power is out for more than a day, discard any medication that should be refrigerated, unless the drug's label says otherwise' and uses a two-hour 40 F food rule; FEMA's December 2023 power-outage fact sheet is newer and differs.

source.title: Make A Plan
source.supports: Four steps: meet with your household (five questions: alerts, shelter, evacuation route, communication plan, kit); assess household needs (ages, responsibilities for assisting others, locations visited, dietary and medical needs, disabilities and access and functional needs, languages, cultural and religious considerations, pets or service animals, school-aged children); document the plan with the free fillable form; practice it. Family meeting place that is familiar and easy to find.

source.title: Build A Kit
source.supports: Basic disaster supplies kit list (water, several days of non-perishable food, radio including NOAA Weather Radio with tone alert, flashlight, first aid kit, batteries, whistle, dust mask, plastic sheeting and duct tape, towelettes and garbage bags, wrench or pliers, manual can opener, local maps, phone and charger with backup battery); additional items (hygiene, medications, eyeglasses, infant supplies, pet supplies, cash, documents, bedding, clothing and sturdy shoes, fire extinguisher, matches, mess kits, paper and pencil, activities); store items in airtight bags in one or two easy-to-carry containers; maintenance (cool dry place, replace expired items, 're-think your needs every year'); kit locations (home, work for at least 24 hours, car).
source.notes: Says to re-think needs 'every year'; the 2020 Are You Ready guide and the CDC pages say every six months. See the cluster notes.

source.title: Ready Emergency Supply List (PDF)
source.supports: Two-page printable checklist linked from the Build A Kit page. Same basic items; says the list is only a starting point and recommends at least two kits: one full kit at home and smaller portable kits at work, in a vehicle or other places where you spend time.
source.notes: The PDF carries no date; the 2024-05 comes from the upload path only.

source.title: Food (emergency food supplies)
source.supports: Store at least a several-day supply of non-perishable food; choose foods your family will eat; remember special dietary needs; example items (ready-to-eat canned goods and a can opener, bars, cereal, peanut butter, dried fruit, juices, non-perishable milk, high-energy and comfort foods, infant food); refrigerator holds cold about four hours unopened; discard perishables above 40 F for two hours or more; do not eat from swollen, dented or corroded cans; use ready-to-feed formula, and bottled or boiled water as a last resort if mixing.

source.title: Evacuation
source.supports: Know your risks, when and where to go, what to bring; build a go-bag so you do not scramble; everyone knows where the bag is and who is responsible; several destinations in different directions; a pet-friendly place because most public shelters allow only service animals; prepare a go-bag to carry on foot or public transport plus supplies for longer trips by car; keep a half tank at all times; one car per family; what to do before leaving; evacuation route may be on foot.

source.title: Car Safety
source.supports: Emergency kit for the car with automobile extras (jumper cables, flares or reflective triangle, ice scraper, car phone charger, blanket, map, cat litter or sand); keep the gas tank full for evacuation or power outages; do not drive through flooded areas.

source.title: Power Outages
source.supports: What an extended outage can disrupt; take an inventory of items that rely on electricity; talk to your medical provider about a power-outage plan for powered medical devices and refrigerated medicines; refrigerator keeps food cold about four hours, a full freezer about 48 hours; discard food at 40 F or above for two hours or more; discard refrigerated medicine if power is out more than a day unless the label says otherwise; generators, camp stoves and charcoal grills outdoors and at least 20 feet from windows, doors and attached garages; CO detectors with battery backup on every level; never heat a home with a gas stovetop or oven.
source.notes: Web page read in full on 2026-10-29. Its medicine line ('discard refrigerated medication if power is out more than a day unless the label says otherwise') repeats the 2020 FEMA guide and is stricter than FEMA's newer December 2023 fact sheet (start-fema-power-sheet), which adds 'call your doctor or pharmacist' and 'only use the medicine until you have a new supply'. Its fridge/food rule is two hours above 40 F; the 2023 sheet says more than 4 hours. Both discrepancies are stated on the three-day-kit page.

source.title: Emergency Alerts
source.supports: Wireless Emergency Alerts (no subscription or charge, distinct sound and vibration, not affected by network congestion, some phones need the setting enabled, older phones may not be capable); Emergency Alert System on broadcast TV and radio; NOAA Weather Radio All Hazards broadcasting 24 hours a day; IPAWS; FEMA App with alerts for up to five locations and shelter finder; local alerting authorities decide what to send and FEMA does not review or approve alerts.

source.title: Financial Preparedness
source.supports: Gather financial, personal and medical records; consider an emergency savings account and keep a small amount of cash in small bills at home because ATMs and cards may not work; obtain property (homeowners or renters), health and life insurance; homeowners insurance does not typically cover flooding; store important documents in a safety deposit box, external drive or the cloud; household identification, financial and legal, medical, insurance and contact lists; direct deposit or Direct Express for federal benefits because disasters can disrupt mail; scam cautions.
source.notes: Mentions the pandemic in a few lines; the page is otherwise generic.

source.title: People with Disabilities
source.supports: Support network and contact list; tell the network where supplies are and consider giving a trusted person a key; plan accessible transportation; voluntary local registries; know more than one dialysis or treatment facility; talk to your doctor about keeping electric medical equipment running and ask your power provider about priority restoration; medical alert tags; communication cards; kit tips by disability (deaf or hard of hearing, blind or low vision, speech disability, intellectual or developmental, mobility including a spare battery and a lightweight manual chair, Alzheimer's and dementia); several days' supply of prescription medicines; extreme-heat cautions; direct deposit.
source.notes: The URL ready.gov/disability redirects here.

source.title: Older Adults
source.supports: 'Take Control in 1, 2, 3' guide (assess needs, make a plan, engage your support network); at least one support-network member should have an extra key, know where supplies are and know how to use lifesaving equipment or give medicine; ask clinics that give routine treatments about their emergency plans and back-up providers; plan transportation if you need help evacuating; copies of Medicaid, Medicare and insurance cards; not all shelters accept pets; direct deposit or Direct Express.
source.notes: The URL ready.gov/seniors redirects here.

source.title: Ready Kids
source.supports: Everyone in the family can help prepare; Ready Kids has sections for kids, teens, families and educators, games, and a family emergency planning collection. The landing page itself carries no instructions.
source.notes: Landing page only. We did not read the sub-pages (kids/make-a-plan, kids/prepare-your-family).

source.title: Low and No Cost Preparedness (graphics collection)
source.supports: Graphic text (English version): look for deals at garage sales and thrift stores for camping gear, tools and cookware; have a family evacuation plan; use the free preparedness resources and the free emergency communication plan form; consider adding older clothing that still fits to the kit; sign up for local emergency alerts.
source.notes: Text is read from the graphic captions on the collection page. The page the graphic points to (ready.gov/low-and-no-cost) was not fetched.

source.title: Stay Connected (Prepare Your Health)
source.supports: Emergency action plan with important phone numbers and at least two meeting places; microchip pets and keep registration current; have multiple ways to communicate, and text messages often go through when calls do not; plan for children, older adults and pets.

source.title: Prescriptions (Prepare Your Health)
source.supports: Talk to your doctor or pharmacist about an emergency supply; keep a list of prescriptions with diagnosis, dosage, frequency, supply needs and allergies; nonprescription drugs; cooler and chemical ice packs for medicines that need chilling; some states have emergency prescription refill laws, so learn yours.
source.notes: Gives no number of days for a medicine supply.

source.title: Making an Emergency Plan (Emergency Preparedness and Disability Inclusion)
source.supports: List of supplies for at least a week; arrange alerts; contact list of the people who support your health, with arrangements for them to check on you directly; several places to go if you evacuate; pictures in the plan if helpful; plan for service animals and assistive technology; backup manual chair; practice the plan, review and update it every year, and share it with the people who support you.

source.title: Building an Emergency Kit (Emergency Preparedness and Disability Inclusion)
source.supports: Batteries and portable chargers for adaptive equipment; communication aids; at least one week's supply of prescription medications and a cooler for refrigerated ones; medical supplies and health documents; extra mobility devices if obtainable; contact list in a watertight container; supplies for pets and service animals; check kits every six months.

source.title: Sheltering and Evacuating (Emergency Preparedness and Disability Inclusion)
source.supports: Keep health-needs information with you and wear medical alert tags; accessible transportation may not be available in an emergency, so contact paratransit or local government ahead of time; tell shelter workers your needs; shelters must be accessible under the ADA; shelters must allow service animals, and under the Fair Housing Amendments Act disaster shelters are required to allow emotional support animals.

source.title: Emergency Kit Checklist: Pregnant Women, Infants, and Children
source.supports: Essential items list; prescription medications of at least a two-week supply; check expiration dates and function every six months; extra water if pregnant or lactating; additions for pregnancy, for an infant (0-12 months) and for a young child (1-5 years) including ID tags, wristbands and memorized phone numbers; the pregnancy list includes emergency birth supplies and a plan with the health care provider.
source.notes: Two-week medication supply differs from the one-week (CDC disability page), several-day (Ready.gov) and 30-day (Red Cross) figures.

source.title: Emergency List for Families With Infants and Young Children
source.supports: Kit contents by feeding method (breast milk, pump, formula); ready-to-feed formula is the safest formula option in an emergency; check the kit monthly so formula matches the baby's current needs; diaper bag contents; items marked with an asterisk are unsafe if they cannot be cleaned with safe water and soap; consider a camp stove and pot for boiling water. Lists 'Infant pain reliever with acetaminophen' with no dosing, age or weight guidance anywhere on the page. Starred items: breast milk storage bags or containers, breast pump and parts, manual pump, powdered formula and preparation materials, pacifiers, bulb syringe.
source.notes: Whole page re-read on 2026-10-30 (about 16,500 characters, no truncation). The 'reviewed' date (2024-02-15) is earlier than the 'published' date (2024-05-15) on the page itself; reproduced as shown. The two-page PDF version of the checklist was not read.

source.title: Older Adults Emergency Preparedness
source.supports: Identify likely disasters and community plans; build a support network and meet with helpers; plan to stay home at least two weeks or evacuate; sign up for local registries if you need help evacuating; back-up plan for power-dependent medical devices and medicines that must stay cold; two ways out of every room; property or renter's insurance; keep at least 30 days of medications and extra assistive items; review, practice and refresh the plan, supplies and documents now and every six months.
source.notes: The American Red Cross is a congressionally chartered nonprofit, not a regulator or government agency. The page shows no date. Fetched and read in full (main content) on 2026-10-29.

source.title: Emergency Preparedness (older adults and people with disabilities)
source.supports: About half of people 65 and older have two or more chronic health problems; at a minimum build a kit with medication, food, water, batteries or chargers, pet and service-animal supplies and shelter locations; ACL's Medical Information Card and Communication Assistance Card; build a support network for communication, transportation and essential care; Eldercare Locator 1-800-677-1116; Disability Information and Access Locator (DIAL); SAMHSA Disaster Distress Helpline 1-800-985-5990; HHS emPOWER data exists to help communities plan for people who rely on electricity-dependent equipment.
source.notes: Page header carries a noindex robots tag. The 'Last modified' date is as printed on the page.

source.title: Multifamily Disaster Preparedness Plan Template
source.publisher: U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD Exchange)
source.supports: Read the introduction, disclaimer, table of contents and first 12 of 79 pages. An optional planning template for owners of multifamily properties; covers resident protection and safety, building protection and business continuity; the table of contents lists resident handouts, an evacuation special assistance form and a go-bag checklist. Supports only the statement that such a template exists. Does not establish any legal duty of any landlord or any HUD requirement.
source.notes: Pages 13-79 were NOT read. The template's own disclaimer says it is a model for owners to adapt, that not all recommendations apply to every building, and that opinions in it do not necessarily reflect HUD's official position. Do not use it as evidence of what any owner is legally required to do. The RAD requirement it mentions was not checked against current HUD rules.

source.title: Assistance for Housing and Other Needs
source.supports: FEMA help applies to presidentially declared disasters and primary residences; rent and lodging expense reimbursement for displaced households; Serious Needs payments for essentials such as food, water, baby formula and medication; accessibility repairs; you may qualify even if you have insurance, after filing a claim; eligibility conditions include citizenship or qualified-alien status and identity verification; apply at disasterassistance.gov, by phone at 1-800-621-3362 or at a Disaster Recovery Center.
source.notes: Main page content read in full on 2026-10-30 (about 6,250 characters). The page calls its eligibility list 'general conditions'; it does not say whether conditions vary by declaration or change over time. We did not read the Individual Assistance Program and Policy Guide it links to.

source.title: Protecting People Who Live or Work in High-Rises
source.supports: Know the exits and fire-safety features of your building; practice your exit route; do not prop stairway or corridor doors open; do not use elevators during a fire; close stair doors behind you; call 911; not all tall buildings meet modern standards; a person who cannot use the stairs should call 911 and be prepared to shelter in place, possibly in a room with the door closed and a wet towel sealing the cracks, or wait on a clear stair landing for help.
source.notes: Whole page re-read on 2026-10-30 via direct download. A blog post written for fire educators; the exit and shelter-in-place messages are about FIRE in tall buildings and say nothing about other hazards. Not the same page as the 'usfa-fire-escape' placeholder in register.json.

source.title: Be Prepared for a Power Outage (FEMA V-1008, December 2023)
source.supports: English two-page sheet (pages 1-2 of a 34-page file) read in full as extracted text: make a plan for refrigerating medicines and powering medical devices; talk to your doctor to plan for medical devices and medication storage; generators, camp stoves and charcoal grills outdoors at least 20 feet from building openings such as windows, doors or garages; never use a gas stovetop, oven, grill or dryer to heat a home; CO and smoke alarms with battery backup; refrigerator keeps food cold about 4 hours, full freezer about 48 hours; throw away refrigerated food above 40 F for more than 4 hours; 'Replace refrigerated medications if the power is out for a day or more, unless the drug's label says otherwise. Call your doctor or pharmacist if you depend on refrigerated medications that have been at room temperature. Only use the medicine until you have a new supply.'
source.notes: Newer than the 2020 FEMA guide and the Ready.gov power-outages web page, which say to discard refrigerated medication after a day and use a two-hour food rule. Pages 3-34 of the file yielded no extractable text (likely translations as images) and were not read. Downloaded directly with curl and converted with pdftotext because Firecrawl had no credits.

source.title: Keeping Food Safe During an Emergency
source.publisher: USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service
source.supports: Refrigerator keeps food safely cold about 4 hours if unopened; refrigerated food should be safe as long as power is out no more than 4 hours; discard perishable food (meat, poultry, fish, eggs, leftovers) that has been above 40 F for 2 hours; coolers and frozen gel packs help if the outage will exceed 4 hours.
source.notes: Search excerpt read 2026-11-01 and the full page text fetched by verify_sources.py on the same day (see audit/start-here/ledger.json for size and hash). Used only to separate the two conditions behind the 4-hour and 2-hour figures. The page shows no date in the text extracted.

source.title: What to Do to Protect Yourself During a Power Outage
source.supports: Carbon monoxide section: never use a generator, pressure washer or other gasoline-powered engine inside the home, basement or garage, or less than 20 feet from any window, door or vent; use an extension cord longer than 20 feet to keep the generator at a safe distance.
source.notes: Search excerpt read 2026-11-02; full page text fetched by audit/start-here/verify_sources.py on the same run (size and hash in ledger.json). Added to cross-check the 20-foot figure from Ready.gov and FEMA. The CDC's wording ('less than 20 feet') and its carbon monoxide basics page ('more than 20 feet') differ slightly from Ready.gov's 'at least 20 feet'; none of them says 20 feet is safe at every site.
